A ‘democratised’ financial crisis is still a crisis
articleContent: Billionaire Mark Walter’s brief ownership stints at the Los Angeles Lakers basketball team (he sold his stake this month) and Chelsea Football Club (where he is seeking to sell too) are unlikely to be mourned. But the flak he got from sports fans is nothing compared with the fallout that may be looming in financial markets.

The deals appear to be linked to a dash for cash related to scrutiny of previously hidden “affiliated investments” between different parts of Walter’s business empire. This, though, may prove more than a one-off event in the wider market. Walter was a pioneer in the now fashionable practice of combining private credit asset managers with life insurers. Some regulators rightly seem nervous about sector-wide problems.

When the global financial crisis blew up nearly two decades ago, there were multiple factors that fuelled it. Many stemmed from an inherent bug of banking. Banks borrow most of their money on a short-term basis, from depositors or in the overnight interbank market, and lend it for more extended periods.

Among the many post-crisis regulatory reforms were a clutch that sought to minimise the systemic risk posed by this “duration mismatch”. One of the resulting structural changes in finance was a shift to lending by “shadow banks” such as private capital groups, which raised their funds not from individual depositors but from so-called limited partners such as global sovereign wealth funds and endowments.

The threat of mass losses for individual bank customers, aka voters, had been one of the main triggers for governments across the globe to bail out banks in 2008. Shifting that risk to sophisticated institutional investors was surely wise all round, policymakers reasoned.

And that, for many years, was how private capital operated — until the inevitable course of financial innovation played out. As more and more banks retreated from corporate lending, new models such as Walter’s, which connected large life assurance cash piles with corporates in search of credit, began to catch on. Private capital group Apollo bought life insurer Athene. KKR acquired Global Atlantic. Before long the symbiosis had become mainstream.

It’s easy to see why. For the private capital groups, they had a new and ready flow of money from life insurance premiums to lend out. For policymakers, the model looked less leveraged than traditional bank lending and less likely to put bank deposits at risk.
There are at least three areas of concern, nonetheless.

First, and most obviously, there hasn’t been a major credit cycle downturn since 2008. Jitters have been evident over recent months, with investors sometimes rushing to exit private credit funds. Public bond markets are jittery too and have sold off sharply in recent months. Given geopolitical tension and persistent inflation, a sharp rise in credit defaults feels overdue.

Second, there is a serious design flaw in partnerships between private credit and insurers, at least for insurance policyholders. As private credit groups have shifted away from relying on capital from institutional investors, who expect to exit after a few years, scrutiny of performance and fees has inevitably decreased. In another conflict of interest, insurers may put too much money into private credit, disregarding good-practice asset diversification.

Third, as the term “shadow banking” suggests, data on the sector and any emerging problems is much harder to come by. There is also little transparency about the many sophisticated ways private credit has found to leverage the underlying assets — with much of that borrowing ultimately finding its way back into the banking system.

The fragmented and often underpowered nature of insurance regulation across different US states, and in offshore centres, means the policing of these risks can be weak. In the case of Walter, it is telling that the scale of hidden affiliated trading has been pursued not by the Delaware insurance regulator but by US prosecutors and the SEC.

If the worst happens, and the Walter saga does presage a broader crisis, financiers believe there would be no sudden shock as there was in 2008. It would be a “long-term democratised problem”, as one bank boss put it to me. In other words, the pain would be spread out over the term of decades-long annuities, with losses on soured loans potentially filtering through to millions of annuity owners as lower payouts.
For those who worry about finance’s societal licence to operate over the long term, that’s no less concerning than the taxpayer bailouts of 2008.
patrick.jenkins@ft.com

title: What happens to suppliers when Germany stops making cars?
articleContent: Sembach, a family-run ceramics company based in Bavaria, has been making parts for the auto industry since the 1970s, including sensors used in combustion engines.

But with an end to fossil fuel-powered cars coming into view and Europe’s car manufacturers under increasing pressure from Chinese electric-vehicle makers, Sembach is making a pivot from motors to medical tech.

“We’re currently witnessing a shift,” said Anna Sembach, the 35-year-old chief executive of the family business and its founder’s great-great-granddaughter. “You can really see that production volumes, especially in the European market, have dropped significantly.”
The company, based in Lauf an der Pegnitz near Nuremberg, manufactured on average about 600mn small parts a year for the auto industry until recently. Now the number is closer to 400mn.

With the company’s sales largely dependent on the struggling auto sector, Sembach made a dramatic change in 2023. The ceramics maker set itself a target of reducing the share of automotive revenues to 40 per cent from 80 per cent by 2033.
The stakes for Sembach are existential. “I don’t know if we’d still be around in 10 years’ time” without the new strategy, she said.

In Germany, the shift from the auto business into sectors with stronger growth prospects is gathering pace, with suppliers exploring areas such as medical technology, robotics and defence. With less work to do in auto factories, the carmakers are seeking to produce goods for other industries.

The pivot reflects pessimism about the prospects for the German auto industry, whose global success was synonymous with the country’s industrial prowess. The sector has shed tens of thousands of jobs since 2019 and is set to keep shrinking as Chinese rivals grow in strength.
The domestic automotive sector is set to lose another 125,000 jobs by 2035, according to the VDA, a German automotive industry lobby group, with the risk to suppliers particularly acute.

Three out of four German suppliers affected by the industry’s structural changes are already making the shift into other businesses, according to a survey by restructuring consultancy FTI-Andersch in November. The biggest interest is in the defence sector, where rising spending commitments by European governments have raised expectations of a boom.

The auto business “doesn’t offer significant growth anymore”, Schaeffler Group chief executive Klaus Rosenfeld told the FT. Schaeffler, a stalwart of the German automotive industry, has restyled itself as a motion-technology company and is setting its sights on new industries such as space, robotics and defence.

Schaeffler is now adapting gears and sensors it made for the auto industry for use in humanoid robots. For the space industry, Schaeffler executives believe they can produce bearings, reaction wheels and power electronics.
The company estimates it can generate 10 per cent of its revenues from defence, robotics and space by 2035.
“This is not going to replace the auto business, but it’s going to give extra growth,” Rosenfeld said, adding that the shift “will give people some optimism that a company can reinvent [itself]”.

Bosch, the world’s largest auto supplier, is looking to diversify. The company has announced plans to cut 22,000 jobs worldwide as its traditional auto business struggles. But it recently said it was expanding into robotics, which executives said could eventually turn into a multibillion-euro business. The Stuttgart-based company reported €91bn in revenues last year.

Even Volkswagen, the world’s second-largest carmaker by volume, is looking to link up with defence companies to offload factories the carmaker no longer needs for auto production. VW has held talks with the maker of Israel’s Iron Dome about using its plant in Osnabrück.

Mercedes-Benz recently signed a memorandum of understanding with drone start-up Tytan to deliver vehicles for mobile air defence units, with chief executive Ola Källenius signalling openness to expanding the carmaker’s military business.

But even fast growth in the defence industry was not enough to make up for the rapid loss of automotive production, said Simon Schnurrer, an auto consultant at Oliver Wyman. Switching industries could offer a way to replace lost volumes for a select number of automotive companies “but it is not sufficient for a large part of the supplier population”, he said.

For Sembach, the experience of meeting the strict specifications of the auto industry made it well suited to making parts for pacemakers and endoscopy technology. But adapting to the medical industry’s smaller volumes meant production at the company’s factories in Bavaria needed to be adjusted. Fewer staff were needed on the production line.

The shift also offered an escape from the relentless price competition and tight margins of the auto industry. “In the automotive sector, every cent is a battleground, whereas that’s not really the case in the medical sector,” Sembach said.
The move away from Germany’s auto industry towards medical equipment had borne some fruit for the company, which recorded record revenues of €23mn last year, Sembach said.
While the market for its products in automotive had shrunk, the medical industry was a “rapidly-growing market, simply because people are living longer”, she said. “That isn’t going away.”

title: JPMorgan eases approach on lending against shares to court AI’s new wealth
articleContent: JPMorgan Chase is relaxing its approach to lending money against shares held by employees and early investors in companies that have recently gone public, as the US bank seeks to win clients from emerging tech giants.

JPMorgan’s typical policy is not to accept as collateral shares in a company that has gone public within the past 135 days. However, it told bankers ahead of SpaceX’s blockbuster initial public offering in June that it would lend against shares in Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company sooner, according to people familiar with the matter.

Bankers inside JPMorgan expect the lender to have a similar approach when Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, goes public, though no final decision has been made. JPMorgan earned $75mn from its role on the SpaceX listing.
JPMorgan’s move underscores the efforts asset managers are making to win business from the huge wealth being generated by the AI boom.
Its policy was already longer than the 30 days that broker-dealers generally wait to lend against shares when they worked on the IPO under US securities rules.
Other banks such as Goldman Sachs will typically not wait longer than the 30-day period before engaging in this type of lending, said people familiar with the matter. Goldman declined to comment.

JPMorgan said the bank’s policy remains unchanged. “Our practices exceed regulatory requirements, and we have always assessed transactions on a case-by-case, client-by-client basis, factoring in elements such as market liquidity,” it said.
Anthropic declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
Top engineers at AI labs can earn millions and sometimes tens of millions of dollars, part of which is company stock.

In the second quarter, Morgan Stanley’s wealth management business took in more than $74bn in net new assets from IPOs, including SpaceX, through its work managing employee equity plans for companies. The bank has said this performance was “not a one-time hit” with a pipeline of future big stock market listings.

Some Anthropic employees are sitting on tens of millions of dollars. Anthropic was valued at $18bn in 2024, and was most recently valued at $965bn. The company said in June it had confidentially filed for an IPO and investors expect the AI start-up to float at a valuation of $2tn or more in October.
Borrowing against shares can be a more popular option than selling for wealthy individuals, to minimise tax impacts.

A crucial question for banks examining collateral quality is how easily it can be liquidated, and private shares are less easily tradeable than public stock. Even after a company has gone public, there can also be lock-up agreements that place restrictions on stock sales. Shares after an IPO can also be more volatile.
Nevertheless, the glut of highly valued tech companies going public represents an enormous opportunity for Wall Street groups looking to manage money for the newly wealthy.

Other wealth management firms have also been working to entice the employees of big AI groups before they go public, cutting fees and hiring staff around Silicon Valley in an attempt to win over workers at OpenAI and Anthropic before their IPOs turn out a new class of millionaires.
Additional reporting by Harriet Clarfelt

title: Melrose faces $100mn compensation payouts after California toxic chemicals scare
articleContent: London-listed Melrose Industries has launched a $100mn compensation scheme after a toxic chemical scare at a plant in California forced the evacuation of residents and businesses.

The incident in May at a GKN Aerospace chemical tank led to the temporary closure of the Garden Grove facility in southern California, after a “thermal issue” was discovered in one of three tanks containing methyl methacrylate, a chemical used to manufacture aeroplane cabin windows.

Melrose, which bought aerospace parts supplier GKN in 2018, also confirmed in an update on Tuesday that the Orange County District Attorney’s Office had closed its criminal investigation into the event.

No injuries, leaks or contamination resulted from the incident, but the plant — which generated £136mn in revenue for Melrose in 2025 — has been running at half its total output capacity since May, which has cost the aerospace and defence group about £6mn a month.
Melrose said GKN had permanently decommissioned the tank involved in the incident “and has made substantial investments in safety enhancements at the facility”.
The FTSE 100 group said it planned to resume full operations at Garden Grove by September 28, “with a phased return to full capacity and customer deliveries during the fourth quarter”.

“The claims programme, which is expected to become effective in the coming weeks and remain open into 2027, will reimburse those eligible for costs associated with the evacuation, including hotel stays, meals, transportation, loss of wages, and loss of use,” Melrose said.
However, claims by emergency services agencies for costs incurred in responding to the incident and potential civil enforcement penalties will be dealt with separately.
Melrose’s shares rose 9 per cent on Tuesday but were still down 17.5 per cent in the year to date.

In its half-year results last month, Melrose said that in addition to the monthly revenue hit from processing lower volumes at Garden Grove, the group expected additional exceptional costs of £25mn to £30mn in the second half of the year. It also paused its £175mn share buyback programme while it assessed the full financial impact of the incident.

title: Berkshire-backed Japanese insurer plots multibillion-dollar deal
articleContent: Tokio Marine, the Japanese insurer backed by Berkshire Hathaway, is closing in on its largest acquisition after months of due diligence on Australian and Canadian targets.
Pursuing a multibillion-dollar international takeover is part of chief executive Masahiro Koike’s push to diversify the operations of one of Japan’s largest financial services companies.

Over the past months, Tokio Marine has reviewed a number of targets including Australia’s Insurance Australia Group (IAG) and Suncorp — two of the country’s biggest general insurers and among its most valuable listed companies — as well as Canada’s Intact Financial Corporation, with a view to launching a deal.
Suncorp and IAG have market capitalisations of about US$14bn (A$20bn) and US$13bn respectively, while Intact is worth about US$34bn (C$47bn).

Two people with direct knowledge of the matter said Suncorp had emerged as the preferred target, with the Canadian company deemed too large. The same people warned that discussions were ongoing and there was no certainty a deal would result.
Shares in Suncorp rose 8 per cent on Tuesday, reducing their decline over the past 12 months to about 8.6 per cent. IAG was up 3.8 per cent.
Tokio Marine said it would not comment on market speculation. Suncorp, IAG and Intact all declined to comment. Some details of Tokio Marine’s plans were first reported by The Australian.

Berkshire Hathaway, which was until recently run by Warren Buffett, acquired a 2.5 per cent stake in the Japanese company in March that also involved an agreement to co-operate on large-scale international M&A.
The plan is for the two groups to make sizeable acquisitions together that use Berkshire’s balance sheet alongside Tokio Marine’s operational expertise and its record in identifying takeover targets.
Since 2008, Tokio Marine has made five large-scale international deals in property and casualty insurance worth roughly $19bn, including paying $7.5bn for US-based HCC — its largest deal to date.

Although it is not clear what Berkshire’s role in a potential takeover would be, said the same people, the deal with the US giant is intended to involve insurance M&A outside Japan that will allow Tokio Marine to preserve firepower for domestic investment.

Tokio Marine was the main insurer to supply chain finance provider Greensill Capital, which collapsed in 2021. Two years earlier the Japanese company had acquired Bond & Credit Co, the Sydney-based outfit that provided billions of dollars of cover to Greensill.
Tokio Marine’s takeover of BCC was part of an aggressive global expansion that included buying out IAG’s 50 per cent stake.
IAG offers a variety of policies such as vehicle and rural insurance in Australia and New Zealand under brands including NRMA and CGU.
Brisbane-based Suncorp also trades under the AAMI and GIO brands and has been seen as a potential target for consolidation after selling its banking arm to ANZ in 2024.
Suncorp posted a net profit of A$1bn, paid a special dividend and announced a share buyback at its annual results this month.

Steve Johnston, the long-serving chief executive, said Suncorp had invested in new IT systems, simplified its business and struck a new reinsurance deal that would reduce earnings volatility and natural hazard risk.
“This result demonstrated that a well-run insurance company can deliver for both customers and shareholders,” he said.
Recommended
Australia has been a hunting ground for Japanese investors for decades, with its energy, logistics, industrial, consumer and real estate sectors the target of high-profile takeover moves.
Australia’s insurers have also been targeted by Japanese rivals, with Daiichi Life and Tokio Marine having acquired smaller players in the past.

Japanese foreign direct investment reached a record $113bn last year, according to a report by law firm Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer and the Australian National University, with 77 transactions completed, including Mitsui’s $5.4bn investment in the Rhodes Ridge iron ore joint venture.
The report said Australia’s life insurance and financial services sectors were attractive to Japanese investors due to the country’s population growth and affluent consumer base.
Additional reporting by Ilya Gridneff in Toronto

title: Private equity growth funds attract record first-half inflows as sector rebounds
articleContent: US private equity funds that invest in fast-growing companies without taking a controlling stake raised a record amount of capital in the first half of this year, in a sign of their strong recovery from a 2023 fundraising slump.

Growth funds attracted $33.2bn in the first six months of this year, the highest first-half total on record and a 36 per cent jump from a year earlier, according to data from Preqin. Fundraising across other private equity strategies grew 20 per cent over the same period.
The surge comes even as the number of growth funds raising capital dipped to 87 in the first half from 96 a year earlier.

Large, established managers and smaller specialist funds are among the beneficiaries of the inflows, helped by surging interest in AI-related companies and valuations that in some cases are still below the highs hit in the industry’s 2021 boom during the coronavirus pandemic.
“I think the recovery is definitely real,” said Jeff Machlin, managing partner of Connecticut-based Wingman Growth Partners, which closed a $215mn growth fund in June, “but it’s selective in nature.”

Fundraising for US private equity growth funds peaked in 2021, when $67bn was raised for the year, as monetary and fiscal stimulus during the coronavirus pandemic helped drive a technology investment rush that pushed valuations sharply higher and often prioritised revenue growth over profitability.

But as doubts grew over whether rapidly expanding companies could ultimately deliver the profits implied by their valuations, investors raced to pull back from growth equity, with fundraising tumbling to just $29bn in 2023.

“The whole asset class got penalised,” said Hugh MacArthur, chair of Bain & Company’s global private equity practice. “Investors basically said: ‘Stop — I don’t know what anybody’s doing, so I’m not investing’.”

A drop-off in initial public offerings and dealmaking meant there were fewer exits available for private investments, which limited the payouts back to investors and reduced their ability to put money to work again in new funds.

However, growth equity fundraising has risen in both of the past two years and is on track to grow again this year. A survey by consultancy McKinsey & Co of 296 institutional investors in January found 46 per cent of respondents planned to increase their allocation to growth private equity in the coming three years. That compared with 35 per cent for buyout funds and 41 per cent for venture capital.

Private company valuations have “come down pretty materially” compared with 2021, said Chris Cavanagh, general partner at Boston-based Guidepost Growth Equity, which raised $521mn for its latest fund in January, adding that investors could now “enter at more attractive multiples”.

The huge success of AI start-ups has also helped make growth equity more attractive, say investors, as pension plans and endowments seek exposure to what they think could be the next technology winner.

“There is more demand from allocators to make sure that they have access within their portfolios to the next OpenAI, Anthropic or SpaceX, to ensure that they’re not kind of missing the boat,” said Luke Riela, who advises institutional investors on private market investments at consultancy Meketa.

However, investors have also been selective in the funds they back, with much of the money flowing into a handful of big funds, which are often more able to absorb large inflows from institutional investors. Three growth funds — including the $10bn Thrive X fund, run by Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital — accounted for more than half of the capital raised in the first six months of this year.

“This is not where the best returns are,” said an executive at a state pension plan that had invested in large growth funds this year, speaking about large funds in general. “This is ‘I think I can safely put $500mn to work’.”

Smaller, specialised growth funds have also found success. Sheldon Lewis, managing partner at San Diego-based Blueprint Equity, said he was able to raise $333mn for a fund focused on early-stage AI-driven software companies, helped by strong returns from its previous funds.
“When you come back to your investors to raise your next fund and you’ve already paid them quite a lot of money, they are obviously a lot more inclined to give you money down,” said Lewis.

Despite the momentum, many growth funds are still struggling to raise capital as exits remain challenging and traditional software, once a major focus for growth equity investment, faces the threat posed by rapid developments in AI.

Sarah Sandstrom, head of North America private equity placement at Campbell Lutyens, a financial advisory, said growth funds launched in 2022 had so far returned virtually no cash to investors, while those launched in 2021 had returned about 60 cents for every dollar invested — low levels by industry standards.
“The last wave of growth investing has yet to really give people confidence that it’s bearing fruit by and large,” she said.
Bruce MacDonald, chief investment officer of the $2.5bn Virginia Commonwealth University Investment Management Company, said he has stayed away from traditional growth funds.
They are “so dependent on software, which is a very risky place to be investing”, he said.

title: Yahoo, the internet’s ‘OG’, wants to win over Gen Z
articleContent: Yahoo wants to convince a new generation of users that one of the internet’s oldest services can be one of the new AI winners, with the Apollo-backed company seeking to develop its brand alongside the launch of an in-house AI tool and consumer products.

Chief executive Jim Lanzone told the FT that the company’s heritage gave it credibility with younger users not alive when it launched in 1994 in a “vintage way”. He described Yahoo as the internet’s “OG” — a slang term meaning “original gangster”.

He argued that familiarity has become an advantage as trust in some newer technology groups has eroded. “There’s something inherently trustworthy about [being] the ‘OG’ of the space,” he added. “We are the original guide to the internet . . . We want to get the brand back out there again.”

Lanzone, who joined Yahoo from Tinder in 2021 shortly after Apollo acquired the company from Verizon, has sought to recast the internet pioneer as a leaner consumer tech group focused on its biggest brands.

The push comes as Yahoo seeks to prove it can carve out a role in the AI era despite having spent years overshadowed by larger rivals.

While the company still reaches hundreds of millions of users through products including Finance, Sports, News and email services, it remains a challenger in search and other core internet services dominated by Google and more AI-native competitors.

Yahoo plans to fully roll out an AI-powered “answer engine” called Scout later this year alongside several editorial and consumer products, part of a broader effort to return the business to growth.

At its peak as a listed company, Yahoo reached a market capitalisation of more than $125bn in January 2000. After a steady decline and subsequent buyouts, Apollo Global Management acquired Yahoo and AOL for about $5bn in 2021. It sold AOL, another dotcom survivor, to Bending Spoons for $1.5bn this year.

Wall Street bankers have viewed Yahoo as a potential candidate for an initial public offering or sale as early as next year. Lanzone declined to comment on any future transaction but said: “To be an attractive company for any investor or acquirer, you just have to be a growth company again, and that’s what we’ve been focused on.”

Lanzone declined to disclose financial details but said the business was “very healthy”, arguing that Yahoo’s established audience and decades of proprietary search, content and user data would help differentiate its AI products from rivals built primarily on models trained using the open web.

The company has chosen not to license its content to train AI models made by rival tech groups, with Lanzone arguing that many of the deals struck between publishers and AI companies are unlikely to prove a durable business model.

Instead, Scout will draw on information from the open web alongside Yahoo’s own archive of content, user data and three decades of search history. Scout uses technology licensed from a range of AI groups.

“We actually didn’t build it by inhaling the internet and creating our answers that way,” said Lanzone. “We have all of our data from the content side, the user side, and 30 years of search history [so] we should have a really interesting set of ingredients for our chefs to prepare great answers.”

Yahoo plans to fund the AI-based answers through advertising, betting that marketers will follow users from conventional search into AI-powered results. “What we really need in this category is for search advertising to cross the chasm to AI answers,” Lanzone said.

Alongside Scout, Yahoo has been expanding its subscription and consumer offerings. Earlier this year, it launched AlphaSpace, an investment platform combining market data, news and analysis for retail investors, and has since added real-time options data.

“We have some surprises up our sleeves that people would be surprised would come from Yahoo,” said Lanzone. “Once you’ve been through the turnaround period, and I think we’re through that now, you get to the fun part, which is we get to innovate on top of the base that we’ve built.”

title: Shein seeks $27bn valuation from Hong Kong IPO
articleContent: Fast-fashion retailer Shein is seeking a $27bn valuation in a Hong Kong listing next week, almost three-quarters below its peak after previous attempts to list foundered amid pushback by regulators.
The China-founded company plans to raise as much as HK$14bn (US$1.8bn) in a September 1 listing.

It is selling 280mn shares for between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50, giving it a market capitalisation of HK$202bn to HK$210bn ($26bn to $27bn), according to a listing notice published by Hong Kong’s stock exchange on Monday. About 90 per cent of the shares will be available to international investors.
Chinese regulators approved the online retailer’s application to list in Hong Kong last month, giving the green light to an initial public offering that has been more than four years in the making.
Shein’s previous attempts to list in New York and London were derailed by opposition from politicians and regulators amid scrutiny of its Chinese supply chain.
The sub-$30bn valuation — previously reported by the FT — compares with a valuation of about $100bn that Shein reached after a private fundraising round in 2022.
The company has the option to sell an additional 42mn shares depending on demand, which could push the total raised to $2bn.

The banks on the deal, led by Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, will collectively receive an underwriting commission of 1.5 per cent of money raised, along with a discretionary 0.75 per cent incentive fee.
That could mean a fee pool of nearly $40mn before the sale of any additional shares.
Recommended

Cornerstone investors — who commit to buying and holding the shares for six months — took roughly a fifth of the listing and comprised mainly Shein’s existing backers, including US private equity firm General Atlantic and Chinese tech giant Tencent.
General Atlantic and investment group Tiger Global both took part in a $1bn funding round in 2022 that valued Shein at $100bn, according to PitchBook.
Chinese private equity firm Boyu Capital took the largest allocation of $150mn, followed by General Atlantic, Tiger Global and Tencent at about $50mn each.

Shein said it planned to spend about 40 per cent of the proceeds on technology, 40 per cent on marketing, 10 per cent on initiatives to “promote corporate responsibility” and the final 10 per cent on general corporate purposes, according to a term sheet seen by the FT.
Separately, Shein’s $80mn acquisition of American clothing brand Everlane is under a national security review by the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US, Bloomberg reported on Monday.
A person familiar with the deal said Shein had submitted the transaction for review after it was rushed through because of Everlane’s financial difficulties.

title: UK backs Devon tungsten mine in effort to secure critical mineral supplies
articleContent: The UK government is backing efforts to revive a tungsten mine in Devon as part of the global race for the critical minerals needed for everything from defence to technology supply chains.

Tungsten West said on Tuesday that the UK’s National Wealth Fund had invested £71mn in its project, comprising a 7 per cent equity stake for £36mn and up to £35mn in debt financing. Under the deal, the government will also have the right to secure up to half of the mine’s annual production.
The funding injection marks a potential turnaround for the miner that has repeatedly warned of its precarious cash position. Tungsten West said in 2023 that it was on the brink of insolvency.
Shares in the London-listed group jumped 17 per cent on the news.
Tungsten West plans to revive the former Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine on the outskirts of Plymouth. The mine stopped producing in 2018 after its previous owner fell into administration.

China dominates the global production of tungsten, a metal used in the aerospace, weapons and tool manufacturing industries. The price of the material has soared since 2025 in response to export restrictions imposed by Beijing and concerns about potential shortages as governments around the world boost defence spending.

Jeff Court, chief executive of Tungsten West, told the FT that the UK government’s investment, combined with the roughly £40mn the company raised earlier this year from investors including Lansdowne Partners, would support the construction and reopening of the mine this year, with full-scale production expected in 2027.
“All that together gives us a lot more than the project needs to get into full phase production, but it’s always good to have some buffer,” said Court.

He added that the company was in “advanced” talks with a refiner that would buy some of the tungsten and process it into a form that industry can use. Court declined to name the refiner but said it was not based in China.
Most refineries are in China with some in Europe and North America.
John Healey, UK chancellor, said: “We are living in a more dangerous world, which is why backing British industry is more important than ever before.”
Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the investment represented “our critical minerals strategy in action.”
Recommended
After resolving the 2023 liquidity problem, Tungsten West warned at the end of 2024 that it had “very limited cash reserves”.

It continued to raise small amounts, but again warned in December that there was “material uncertainty” about its ability to continue as a going concern and that it had been close to running out of cash.
Court said the company had been at a “very different” stage during that period, when it was still studying the project ahead of fundraising to bring it online.
But Court said Tungsten West had upgraded the project and its processes since then, and noted that the price of tungsten had also skyrocketed.
“The key for us is to get producing and start product going out the gate and start topping up our funding with revenue,” he said.

The company was in talks with potential buyers about a possible “price floor”, or minimum guaranteed price for the mined material, he added. But Tungsten West would be able to operate even if prices fell, since it was “at the very low end of the cost curve”, he said.

title: Burnham rules out early election as he admits UK faces ‘challenging’ financial outlook
articleContent: Andy Burnham has admitted that Britain faces a “challenging” financial outlook and said he would not create political and economic turmoil by calling an early election.

The prime minister, speaking on a visit to Kyiv, said on Monday he would do what he could to help people with their daily living costs but suggested he would not take risks with the economy or adopt policies that pushed up interest rates.
Burnham stopped short of ruling out tax increases in the Budget on October 28 and said his policies would be “funded”.
“Obviously people can see the challenging nature of the financial outlook and we will approach it prudently and carefully,” he told LBC. “We will always make sure that we put people’s security first.
“We won’t take risks with people’s finances or their pensions or homes. But we will, at the same time, try and help with the cost of living.”
Asked by ITV News about whether the public would have to accept higher taxes to pay for commitments on housing, social care and defence, he replied: “They don’t necessarily need to accept that.”
Burnham repeated his promise that he would stick to Labour’s general election manifesto promise not to increase rates of income tax, value added tax or employee national insurance.

Some in the City of London fear that chancellor John Healey could turn to business or wealth creators for extra tax revenue, but Burnham said that he did not want to undermine confidence in the economy.
“I will do what I can, but I won’t be unrealistic,” he told ITV News. “I am going to try my best as we go through the autumn to bring people together, to get some confidence going.
“We have had some early signs that there is more confidence in the economy. I want to build that confidence through the Budget working with the chancellor.”
Recommended
Burnham gave his most explicit rejection of the idea that he might capitalise on an early “bounce” in his poll ratings — with Labour edging ahead of Reform — by holding an early election.
“I am focused on the needs of the country and not party-political interests,” he said. “I am not going to call an election.

“I said outside Downing Street that I would do politics differently, that I would try to bring people together and focus on problem-solving rather than point-scoring. I am ruling it out right in front of you.”

title: Britain gains access to Ukraine battlefield data
articleContent: Britain will become the first foreign country to gain access to a vast trove of Ukrainian battlefield data used to train AI models to identify and strike Russian targets under a broad technology-sharing partnership.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the AI partnership on Monday in Kyiv, opening Ukraine’s Avengers Labs data platform to British researchers and technology companies.
The database draws on millions of observations collected by thousands of cameras and sensors deployed across Ukrainian battlefields.

The announcement came on Burnham’s first overseas trip as prime minister, during which he vowed to maintain the UK’s full support for Kyiv and denounced “outrageous” threats against Britain by Moscow.

Burnham, speaking on the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence, shrugged off recent warnings from Moscow and said: “Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine.”

Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence says Avengers Labs now processes more than 100,000 drone video streams a month and detects about 70 per cent of enemy targets appearing in the imagery. Earlier versions were reportedly identifying about 12,000 pieces of enemy equipment per week.

The data comes from what Ukraine’s MoD refers to as its Universal Military Dataset: a huge collection of real combat imagery, mostly from drones and acoustic sensors, that has been organised and manually labelled.

It is used to train machine-learning models that can recognise and classify battlefield targets such as tanks, drones and artillery pieces, part of Ukraine’s rapid development of increasingly autonomous weapons during more than four years of war.

“High-quality, labelled battlefield data is one of the biggest constraints on developing reliable AI for autonomous systems,” said Misha Nestor, chief product officer for Swarmer, the Ukrainian drone software company. “Ukraine has accumulated something that is extremely difficult to replicate anywhere else: large volumes of data generated under real combat conditions.”

Until now this data has been shared only with domestic companies, giving Ukrainian drone makers a competitive edge over foreign rivals, whose computer vision models were often trained using synthetic data and did not perform so well in combat.

Britain’s military is understood to be particularly interested in data gathered by acoustic sensors placed throughout Ukraine and used to identify incoming Russian drones. Properly trained, these sensors can be far more accurate than radar and could be used to defend military installations and critical infrastructure.

Kyiv first announced it would allow international partners access to the dataset in March, offering “the opportunity to train their AI models on real data from modern warfare”, according to Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s defence minister at the time. In return, Ukraine would gain “faster progress in the development of autonomous systems and new technological solutions for the front”, he said. Zelenskyy sacked Fedorov in July.

The agreement with the UK is part of a wider technology swap intended to marry Ukraine’s battlefield experience and unique wartime data sets with Britain’s universities, AI researchers and technology companies.
Burnham said the deal “will bring together Ukraine’s unrivalled operational experience with Britain’s world-class AI ecosystem”.

It follows Burnham’s announcement that European missile joint venture MBDA would be permitted to release classified information on British components of advanced missiles to help establish assembly lines in Ukraine.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the decision to share technology on the Scalp missile with Kyiv had been received “extremely negatively” by Moscow, which last week warned of unspecified “consequences” for Britain over its support for Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russia.
Recommended

The UK “methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire and hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process”, Peskov told reporters on Monday, according to the Interfax state news agency.

Speaking at the end of his visit to Kyiv on Monday, Burnham was asked by ITV News whether he would seek to persuade countries such as Spain and Greece to hand over stocks of Patriot missiles to help defend Ukraine.
“It’s not for us to say that,” he said. “It’s a matter for those countries first and foremost, but obviously we will use our influence.”
Asked if people in Britain should be worried that the UK was being dragged into the conflict, Burnham replied: “No, we’re not doing anything different. This is continuity.”

title: UK seeks to tighten security of supply chains after Iran-linked cyber attack
articleContent: The UK government is seeking to change the law so it can block companies from buying products from high-risk suppliers, in a move that comes shortly after a hacking group shut down a small energy facility.

Ministers could demand companies in critical sectors such as energy, healthcare and telecoms take extra security measures such as implementing a phased removal of certain vendors or be banned from acquiring technology from them, under proposals announced on Monday.

The vulnerability of key UK infrastructure was highlighted by Sunday’s revelation that hackers thought to be linked to Iran had forced a small gas plant offline. The National Cyber Security Centre has also warned that companies must do more to guard against cyber attacks.

The government’s plans were introduced via amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience bill and are subject to parliamentary approval. They will seek to safeguard the supply chains of companies, which are often used as a “soft underbelly” by hackers seeking to target larger groups.
Baroness Liz Lloyd, cyber security minister, said the new powers meant the government could act “before a threat materialises, not just after the damage is done”.

“This is about staying ahead of a growing threat, and giving the public confidence that the everyday services we depend on like water and energy supplies, our transport network and hospitals are protected,” she said.

The proposals could pose challenges for energy companies, which are heavily reliant on supplies from China, which manufactures more than 90 per cent of the world’s solar panels and dominates supplies of batteries and electric vehicles.

“The implication is that we will end up spending more money to get the same amount of stuff,” said one energy industry executive. “There are alternatives but they are more expensive and they take longer.”
The cyber bill, which was introduced last year, would force regulated companies to report significant attacks to the NCSC within 24 hours and deliver an incident report within 72 hours.
Regulated companies would also face fines if they fail to adhere to a framework covering issues such as data protection and staff training.

title: Reform UK’s ‘Farage Fest’ went ahead without permission from council
articleContent: The organisers of “Farage Fest”, a rally held to celebrate the Reform UK leader’s victory in the Clacton by-election, could face “potential enforcement” from the local council after they hosted the event without permission.

Tendring District Council, which is controlled by a coalition of independents, Labour and the Liberal Democrats, said a late temporary event notice was unsuccessfully submitted in relation to an event on August 13 — the day Nigel Farage won the vote in his seat of Clacton — at Great Oakley Airfield in Harwich, Essex.

“This notice was refused, and a counter-notice served, as it was not submitted within the statutory timescales required under the Licensing Act 2003. No authorisation was therefore granted under a late temporary event notice for the event,” said Lisa Hastings, the council’s corporate director for law and governance.
She added that she had no further comment on any potential council investigation “as the matter may now involve potential enforcement considerations”.
The potential investigation was first reported by independent journalist David Hollas.
The Reform UK leader did not attend the Clacton by-election count, claiming he was told by police about an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”.

But Farage was present at the rally, where he told the crowd of around 600 that he had secured a “convincing, overwhelming win”, having beaten satirical candidate Count Binface by 12,784 votes. News of his victory was met with chants of “Nigel, Nigel, Nigel”.
Video footage of the event showed a band playing against the backdrop of a screen displaying the words “Farage Fest”, a bar featuring branded pint glasses, fire pits, a Ferris wheel and yurts.
Recommended
Temporary event notices are required for activities including selling alcohol and providing entertainment on unlicensed premises.
A photo of an invitation to the event, seemingly authored by Farage, said it would start at 11pm, “with live music and big screens showing the results as they land” and “food and drink throughout”.
Government guidance states that organisers who fail to obtain a TEN and still carry out a licensable activity can be fined, face up to six months’ imprisonment or both.
People close to Reform said the event was invite only and did not require licensing. They added that a notice was submitted on a precautionary basis although there was no need for it.
A party spokesperson said: “Reform UK are confident that no rules were broken and the event was conducted in accordance with the law.”

The Clacton by-election was triggered by Farage in what he said was an attempt to “stick two fingers up” at the “establishment” after the launch of a parliamentary probe into a £5mn gift he received before the 2024 general election from a Thailand-based crypto entrepreneur, Christopher Harborne. The main parties refused to take part, leaving Farage to run against a field of 33 novelty and independent candidates.

title: Top UK university graduates owe the most in student loans
articleContent: Graduates of Britain’s top universities have the highest debt on the most contentious student loan plan, sparking new claims of a “tax on ambition”.

The average Russell Group alumnus repaying a Plan 2 loan owes £52,412, thousands of pounds more than graduates from other institutions, according to FT analysis of the first detailed official data on debts by university.
Some of the difference is likely to be due to longer courses and lower dropout rates at top universities, along with higher costs for students who are more likely to live away from home.

But experts also pointed to the impact of interest rates, which increase by up to 3 percentage points for higher-earning graduates, leaving those who go on to well-paid jobs struggling to pay down their balances.

Oliver Gardner, founder of the student loans campaign Rethink Repayment, said the data from the Student Loans Company, which was provided to the FT under freedom of information laws, highlighted how “even graduates who go into relatively well-paid professions are seeing their loan balances soar despite making significant monthly repayments”.
He called this a “tax on ambition” that “is trapping millions of ambitious young people in a vicious cycle of ever-increasing student loan debt”.
Anger has been simmering for months about the Plan 2 loan system, for those who started undergraduate degrees between 2012 and 2022.

In July the cross-party House of Commons Treasury Committee accused ministers of mis-selling loans to young people and urged a reversal of a decision by former chancellor Rachel Reeves to freeze at £29,385 the threshold at which graduates start to repay 9 per cent of their salary.
Lord William Hague and Lord Chris Smith, the chancellors of Oxford and Cambridge universities respectively, have also called for reforms to the system.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
When she was appointed education secretary last month by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Lucy Powell said the issue of Plan 2 loans was “top of my in tray”, criticising “egregious” interest rates.
However, the Treasury has warned that reform could cost more than £5bn and cautioned that other areas of public spending, such as the NHS and early years, should take priority.
Data from the Student Loans Company on outstanding Plan 2 balances by institution showed wide variation in debts.

Former students of the Royal Veterinary College have the highest average debt at £86,979, reflecting the five-year veterinary degree compared with the three years standard for most undergraduate courses in England. The lowest debts are among those who used Plan 2 loans to attend adult education colleges, typically for shorter periods.

Among larger institutions the lowest average debt is among graduates of the Open University, which charges fees based on modules and whose students study remotely, at £11,194. The highest is at Imperial College London, where degrees are often over four years, running to £63,075.

Overall, borrowers from the 24 research-intensive universities that make up the Russell Group have an average outstanding balance of £52,412, compared with £45,498 across all higher education institutions and £47,777 for graduates of universities that belong to MillionPlus, the advocacy group for post-1992 universities.

Some graduates will have been making repayments for more than a decade, but the outstanding balances are similar to the £47,730 average debt of those who graduated this summer under the replacement Plan 5 scheme.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Hollie Chandler, director of strategic policy at the Russell Group, said: “Higher average debt at Russell Group universities may reflect that more students are completing courses lasting more than three years, like medicine, dentistry or engineering, and continuing into postgraduate study.
“Russell Group students are also typically more likely to live away from home, which involves higher living costs and access to bigger maintenance loans,” she added.
But Chandler said it was “clear that many graduates feel the current system is challenging” and that it was “important the system offers graduates stability, transparency and fairness”.

Nick Hillman, of the Higher Education Policy Institute, cited the same factors but said that, since Russell Group graduates tended to earn more, some of the higher debt “could be because the full interest rate applies only if you’re on a pretty decent salary”.

Unlike the previous and subsequent loan plans, where interest is charged at retail price inflation, interest on Plan 2 loans starts at RPI when borrowers’ income is below £29,385 and rises to RPI plus 3 percentage points once earnings are over £52,885.
Scottish universities, which also have four-year degrees and charge English and Welsh students higher fees, also have high average balances, led by St Andrews at £65,282.
The data covers Plan 2 undergraduate debt among those eligible to repay because they have graduated or dropped out, but does not include Plan 3 loans taken out for postgraduate study.
Despite concern over loans, a record number of students will start university this autumn, with acceptances at more selective universities rising fastest in this year’s A-level results.

Hillman said: “The story about student loans is a story about 30-something professionals. We’ve had three months of horror stories about student loans and demand for higher education is up not down. It has no bearing on 18-year-olds.”

Vivienne Stern, chief executive of Universities UK, the lobby group, said: “Studying for a degree is an investment. For the majority of graduates it pays off through higher average earnings, reduced likelihood of unemployment and a wider range of opportunities.
“While the investment is significant, the loan system means you only pay when you are earning, and at a rate that is designed to be affordable,” she added.

The Department for Education said: “We know the student loan system we inherited is broken and unfair, and some graduates feel the weight of this more strongly. We will continue to look for ways to make the system fairer for students, graduates and taxpayers in a financially sustainable way.”

title: Starmer considered letting 100,000 young Europeans come to UK every year
articleContent: Sir Keir Starmer was looking at giving EU students “home fees” access to British universities and allowing up to 100,000 young Europeans into the UK each year as part of an ambitious economic plan taking shape in the dying days of his premiership.

Britain’s secret negotiating strategy for an EU summit — revealed to the FT by officials involved in drawing it up — was intended to unlock a deal to ensure UK companies were not hit by a new Brussels Made in Europe policy or new steel tariffs.

Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, is looking afresh at the prospective deal between the two sides at a Brussels summit now scheduled for the autumn. The meeting was originally due to take place on July 22, two days after Starmer was forced out of Downing Street.

The revelation of Starmer’s negotiating plan — confirmed by three UK officials preparing the postponed July summit — will be seen as a benchmark by pro-European Labour MPs to assess the ambition of Burnham’s own fledgling EU policy.
Downing Street said on Monday that Burnham had told António Costa, European Council president, during a visit to Kyiv that “the UK had to be bolder in terms of getting closer to the bloc”.

Details of a proposed youth experience scheme remain by far the biggest stumbling block at the summit and Labour officials stressed that ministers in the new Burnham administration were “taking stock” of where negotiations got to under Starmer. “To be clear this isn’t current government policy,” said one.

As time ran out on Starmer’s premiership, London mooted with Brussels a cap on young EU citizens coming to Britain under the time-limited and reciprocal visa scheme at about 50,000. But privately, UK officials said that number could have risen to 100,000 in exchange for summit concessions from Brussels.

Burnham is sensitive to accusations of being soft on migration and has said that every policy of his new administration must meet the “Makerfield test” — that is, to be acceptable to voters in his largely white, working-class constituency in the north of England.

Crucially, the UK side under Starmer was also prepared to agree at a later stage to EU demands that European students be able to study at UK universities for the same fees as home students rather than at international rates that can be as high as £30,000 a year.

British officials argue that “home fees” were not on the table in May 2025 at the first EU-UK summit under Starmer’s premiership, which set in train work for the upcoming summit, and are a “new” demand that should be accompanied by a new offer from Brussels.

One British official said: “This was a new demand from the EU and so it would not have been part of the first package. But we would have been prepared to look at it in a future package, in exchange for something big on the economic side, such as being inside Made in Europe.”

Brussels is proposing to limit public contracts and subsidies for new technologies, such as electric vehicles and clean energy technologies, to manufacturers based in Europe and some trade partners under Made in Europe rules.

While the UK would have some access to the scheme under the proposal, cars for corporate fleets and small EVs would have to be assembled inside the bloc to be eligible for public procurement and subsidies. Corporate fleets make up 60 per cent of new car sales in Europe.

The proposal has sparked an outcry from Britain’s car industry. Nissan has warned it would put the future of its Sunderland site at risk, while BMW’s Mini plant in Oxfordshire would also be hindered by the move.

Meanwhile, a steel “safeguard” measure that drastically cut tariff-free imports of steel on July 1 to the EU is also endangering British steel production and has led to fierce UK lobbying.
Rachel Reeves, then chancellor, insisted in Cabinet this year that any EU deal ensured that Britain was fully included in new Brussels initiatives and did not suffer any new tariffs.
“Keir, Rachel and Nick Thomas-Symonds [former European relations minister] were pushing it very hard,” said one official.

Another official said the cost of any extra state subsidies to UK universities would have been “massively outweighed” by the wider economic advantages of such a deal. “It would have been a footnote,” said the official.
Recommended
One European official said a proposed second round of negotiations in which the UK would gain access to the Made in Europe scheme in return for home fees for European students was unlikely.
“It sounds very British to me,” said one EU diplomat. “Win as much as possible and then make concessions rather vague and come at a later stage.”
Three EU diplomats told the FT that a number of member states had insisted that home tuition fees be part of the reset deal and were opposed to approving anything without them.

The European Commission, the bloc’s executive arm, told EU ambassadors at a private meeting in July that it stressed that lower tuition fees should be part of the youth experience scheme and that the UK should offer a large quota, according to people briefed on the conversation.

The UK government declined to comment on “ongoing negotiations”, adding: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy and unlock growth in every postcode.”

The Melody of Things — rediscovery of a dormant passion
articleContent: Nadia Beard, like me, is a professional writer and amateur pianist whose passion for music led her to return as an adult to where she had left off in her keyboard studies so many years before. That’s only one reason why Beard’s enthralling memoir, The Melody of Things, moved me so deeply.
Beard, who is the managing editor of the news organisation Coda Story, frames her musical homecoming as a journey of personal rediscovery, after turning away from music after university.

Until then, “playing the piano and cello was the core of my life,” she recounts. Growing up in the south-east of England, a shared love of music had connected her to her beloved grandmother, who made sure Beard and her sister learnt to play the piano, and her ability had proven strong enough to earn her a private school scholarship.

But by 30, she had become consumed by her journalistic career. So much so that she surprised herself when, on a visit to friends in Germany, she discovered a grand piano in an otherwise empty room and on an impulse sat down and began to play. The remembered fragments of Handel and Schumann her fingers produced left her amazed and elated. Just as astonished were her friends, who had no idea she had ever played at all.

“Their surprise stood as a daunting testament to how completely I’d neglected music,” she writes. Even more potent was the rush of emotions that sprang from creating music through her own efforts, which she seductively describes as “the elusive, addictive feeling I recognized as that which also braids itself through the first moments of falling in love.”

Music had hooked her once again. No matter that her technique had atrophied. In the chapters that follow she records how, as if following a siren call to recapture a lost love, she pursued her passion.

She began almost immediately, for the next year and a half squeezing in three hours at the piano daily before and after her full-time editorial job, not caring that the gruelling schedule blotted out the possibility of a social life. Her first priority was to prepare the audition programme of works by Bach, Beethoven, and Scriabin that she hoped would earn her entrance to a one-year course at the music conservatoire in Tbilisi, Georgia.

Yet when she attended a bucolic springtime piano residency in France to prepare for the audition, she admitted she felt like an “imposter” beside the many accomplished musicians there. But she persevered, reflecting, “What an uncanny resemblance music lessons can bear to therapy,” when her piano coach counselled her “to get out of her own way.”

The acceptance letter arrived in the summer of 2020. She jubilantly viewed the coming school year as “a starting point, the beginning of an attempt to deepen my relationship to music, to heighten it, to make it mean something.” Nor was she deterred by the need to move to an unfamiliar country or the taxing number of hours needed to continue her editorial job remotely while also putting in needed practice hours.

Still, she could not let go of memories of her teenage self, nonchalantly skipping practice hours and “assuring myself and others I wasn’t good enough” to pursue a professional career. Preoccupied by such thoughts, she could barely answer the first question her conservatoire music teacher Manana Gotsiridze asked her: what had brought her to study there. Only after a long pause could she reply, almost inaudibly, “Because I love music.”

For the nurturing Gotsiridze that was enough. “Choose the music you love, and I’ll teach you how to play it,” she said. But Beard’s self-doubt persisted, and the re-emergence of her years-long battle with stage fright did not help. Her fears became reality when, soon after beginning her studies, she was given the opportunity to play the very piano her hero the Soviet superstar Sviatoslav Richter had performed on when visiting Tblisi years before. Beard unravelled almost immediately, her fingers flailing for the right notes, only to find the wrong ones. “While I began this year as a pianist, I might not end it as one,” she worried.

Enter soon after the easygoing Canadian cellist Arlo. As romantic or musical partners, they at first seemed totally mismatched, he as nonchalant about the need for practice as she was zealous about it. But his good-natured exuberance buoyed her confidence, persuading her to begin playing first for small groups, then larger ones. Although Arlo leaves to return to Canada, Beard remains, refining her musicality as well as her technique with the steadfast Gotsiridze. She completes her year — and her memoir — with the self-assurance to perform as a soloist with a small chamber ensemble in Europe. She has learnt to face the music, and has taught her readers how to withstand the wrong notes even as we find the melodies that sustain us.
The Melody of Things: On Returning to Forgotten Joys by Nadia Beard Faber £18.99, 256 pages

title: Swimming in the shadow of Scottish castles
articleContent: This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Edinburgh

Among the many pleasures of travelling in Scotland, few leave a more lasting impression than coming across a striking view of one of the nation’s venerable castles and delving into its rich history. And there is nothing like a nice swim in Scotland’s clear waters to make a day even more memorable. Fortunately from my base in Edinburgh, it is easy to combine all three pleasures.

Many of Scotland’s finest castles are built on the scenic shores of its lochs, rivers or sea, locations that often made them much easier to defend. Some were specifically built to guard strategic waterways or to provide secure bases for maritime power. Almost all have grand tales to tell of events from their often tumultuous past. And while Scottish waters can be a little chilly, I have always found that taking a dip gives a visceral sense of entering the landscape and often a fresh perspective on even familiar scenes.

So-called “wild swimming” is increasingly popular in Scotland, where broad rights to roam* mean you are unlikely to be prevented from entering most bodies of water as long as you judge it safe and cause no damage or disturbance to wildlife. I have enjoyed swimming near dozens of historic castles all around Scotland. Here are four of the best such swims to try within easy distance of Edinburgh.

One of Scotland’s most imposing medieval fortifications, Tantallon Castle stands atop a high promontory jutting out into the Firth of Forth about an hour’s drive east of Edinburgh. It’s now a very substantial ruin, and ticket-bearing visitors can in summer easily enter the castle from its landward side. But instead of the standard visit, why not take the more challenging approach along the rocky coast to the castle’s east and, if conditions permit, a short swim out into the Forth? This will give you an impressive perspective of the castle’s natural and man-made defences.

The steep cliffs that guarded the castle on its seaward sides, together with the wide dry moat, grand gatehouse and thick curtain wall of rose-red sandstone that shielded it to the south, made Tantallon a bastion from which even royal authority could be defied. In 1528, a siege led by King James V against the rebellious Archibald Douglas, the 6th Earl of Angus, failed to take the fortress after its walls withstood a 20-day bombardment by royal cannon. Never before in Scotland’s history, crowed Douglas afterward, had such “pane travell expensis and diligence” (pain, travel, expense and diligence) been expended unsuccessfully for the “wynnyng of ane house” (winning of a house).

In standing his ground at Tantallon, Douglas was following the example of his 14th-century ancestor, Margaret, Countess of Angus and Mar. A widowed heiress to estates in Scotland’s north-east, Margaret lived in the castle as the mistress of the first Earl of Douglas and mother of his son. But her position became precarious when the earl and his successor died and she was ordered to return Tantallon to its feudal superior, the Earl of Fife — son of the king and guardian of the kingdom.

Instead of meekly submitting, Margaret gathered local gentry and kinsmen at Tantallon, where they held out through the winter of 1388-89 until Fife cut a deal, promising to allow the countess to remain in the castle and to support her, her men and her lands “agayns ony that wald wrang thaim” (against any that would wrong them). The accommodation secured the positions of Margaret’s local supporters and cleared the way for her to establish her illegitimate son George as the first of a new line of earls of Angus. It also demonstrated the influence and authority that independent-minded aristocratic women could exercise in a male-dominated and often violent age.

Tantallon’s walls were eventually humbled by the more modern artillery of Oliver Cromwell during the English dictator’s conquest of Scotland in 1651, but the castle’s ruins were to fire the imaginations of author Walter Scott and painter Alexander Nasmyth in the 19th century.

Nasmyth’s view of the castle from the coast, complete with stormy seas and a shipwreck, is a masterpiece of Scottish Romantic painting. For a similar perspective and a wonderfully scenic swim — though only in much calmer weather — take a bus or drive to Seacliff Beach. The nearest bus stop is at Auldhame Farm and there is paid parking at the beach. From Seacliff, walk westwards past the little old harbour carved in the rocks. Be careful not to pass any headland while the tide is rising to ensure you can easily return. The view of Tantallon becomes ever more dramatic as you approach. Website; Directions

Another clifftop fortress, this time an hour and a half’s drive north-east of Edinburgh, St Andrews Castle was for centuries the residence of influential Catholic clerics before becoming a battleground in the Protestant Reformation that wracked Scotland in the 16th century. It was here in 1546 that Cardinal David Beaton presided over the show trial of evangelical preacher George Wishart, who after his conviction was strangled and burned at the stake outside the castle walls. Months later, the castle was seized by vengeful local lairds and evangelicals, who killed Beaton and hung his body from the walls. The fitful siege that followed drew the attention of England, which supported the Protestant rebels, and Catholic France, Scotland’s traditional ally and the birthplace of Scotland’s dowager queen, Mary of Guise, the mother of Mary Queen of Scots.

Provisions sent by sea to the besieged castle by England’s Henry VIII helped the rebels hold out for more than a year, but it was France’s intervention that proved decisive. In July 1547, King Henry II of France secretly dispatched a small fleet to St Andrews under a brilliant Italian commander equipped with detailed information of Scotland’s coastal waters. A few hours of intense bombardment from the sea and land broke the walls of the castle and the will of its defenders. The assault was, in the words of historian Jane E A Dawson, a “masterclass in the swift reduction of a fortified position”.

For a sense of the sight that would have greeted the arriving French fleet, take a bus or drive to St Andrews and walk to the Castle Sands, a beach below the fortress. There is a well-used though dilapidated tidal pool (swimmable in when the tide is out), but confident swimmers can venture further out for a better view of the castle’s seaward cliffs and walls. Website; Directions

This venerable building is a fine example of the strong verticality of form that makes Scottish tower houses such a distinctive and picturesque contribution to the national landscape. More seriously fortified than many such towers, it was likely built in the late 14th or 15th century and stands on a precipitous slope above the River Tweed about an hour’s drive south of Edinburgh. Viewed from the water, it has an impressive monumentality only slightly relieved by its irregular scattering of windows.

Like Tantallon, Neidpath fell victim to Cromwell’s 17th-century artillery, which emphatically demonstrated the obsolescence of defensive architecture across Scotland. But unlike the more massive coastal castle, Neidpath continued to be occupied afterwards. It even had a brush with the new thinking of the Scottish Enlightenment, when in 1795 it became the residence of Adam Ferguson, a historian and philosopher widely seen as a founding father of modern sociology.

Ferguson, who rented the property from the Duke of Queensberry, was charmed by the beauty of the castle’s situation. “The woods, the hills, and the river, are Elysian, and the atmosphere all composed of vital air,” Ferguson wrote, expressing sentiments likely to be shared by a modern visitor. That was in summer, however, and like many castle residents who lack serving staff or adequate heating, he found winter conditions tougher. Ferguson was as much a master of his feelings as any Stoic, a biographer recounted, “but the discomforts attendant upon his residence at Neidpath were a sore trial for his philosophy”.

To enjoy Neidpath from the water on a warm day, take a bus or drive to Peebles and from there follow the easy circular walk starting on the south side of the Tweed, crossing the river by the old viaduct and returning eastward to pass directly below the castle. There is a popular swimming spot a little west of Neidpath with a fine view of the castle on its leafy bank, but for maximum visual drama use the little beach below it. From there, its ancient walls loom starkly overhead against the sky. The current can be brisk and the river should never be entered when it is in spate. Website; Directions

The end of the St Andrews siege did not end the struggle to decide Scotland’s religious and diplomatic loyalties. The resourceful Mary of Guise fought hard as regent to maintain Catholicism and ties with France. But by the time her daughter Mary Queen of Scots returned from France to exercise her monarchy in August 1561, Protestantism was dominant among the population and the fractious nobility, and ties with Protestant England increasingly close. Though the younger Mary’s religious tolerance and personal charisma initially stabilised her reign, less than seven years later a series of political mis-steps and disastrous alliances would leave her in ignominious imprisonment in Lochleven Castle.

Situated on a small island half a mile from the shore of the expansive Loch Leven, about halfway between Edinburgh and St Andrews, the castle seemed the most secure of prisons to the “Confederate Lords” who deposed Mary. Weakened by defeat and the traumatic miscarriage of twins, and under extreme psychological pressure, she agreed to abdicate in favour of her infant son, James. But as soon as her health returned she began to plan her escape. Less than a year after being ferried into captivity, she had won over some younger members of the Lochleven Castle household. One, a page known as “Little Willie”, agreed to row her across the loch. On May 2 1568, Willie sabotaged all but one of the castle’s boats, then opened the main gate for Mary with a key purloined from the laird while he and his family were dining. By the loch shore, another household admirer was waiting for them with horses.

Within days, an army of 6,000 men had mustered to Mary’s support. But panicking after defeat in a battle near Glasgow, she fled to England — a decision that led to long captivity and eventual execution. It was a sad end to one of history’s most romantic royal escapes.

Partial draining in the 19th century reduced Loch Leven somewhat and increased the size of the island, but the sight of the castle across the water would still be recognisable to its regal former prisoner. To enjoy the view from the water, take a bus or drive to Kinross and walk to Kirkgate Park, where there is a pleasant sandy beach. Toxic blue-green algae can be an issue in the loch in summer months, so check boards for any warnings or ask locals for guidance, and avoid the water if there is any sign of a bloom. Website; Directions

*Note: Scottish law gives broad rights to responsible access to land and waters, but “wild” swimming is always at your own risk. To avoid unseen hazards and potentially dangerous cold-water shock, always enter the water cautiously. Tailor any swim carefully to your ability. Check ahead for strong currents, tides, algae infestation or pollution

title: The seven stages of a facelift
articleContent: What An ultrasound treatment that works by directing micro-focused sound waves deep into the skin’s structural layers – including the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), a connective layer that sits between muscle and fat. This thermal energy stimulates fresh collagen production deep within the skin, gradually tightening, lifting and firming the jaw, chin, neck and brows. It remains the only FDA-cleared ultrasound device for skin lifting, though other well-regarded options exist, including Sofwave and HIFU.

Who Anyone who has noticed the creeping effects of skin laxity, which typically emerges as collagen begins to deplete. Safe for all skin tones, it is reportedly used by Jennifer Aniston and Helena Christensen.

What to expect After a conductive gel is applied, a practitioner moves the device over the face for between 30 and 90 minutes. Some spots may feel tingly or pleasantly warm, while more sensitive areas, such as those over bone, the neck or around the eye, may feel a piercing heat that quickly builds then is over in seconds. Results emerge gradually over three to six months and last for a year afterwards.
Downsides Tenderness and swelling are standard. Less common risks include temporary nerve irritation, which can cause facial asymmetry, and fat loss that could accentuate signs of ageing.
