Dr Lee Seung-Hyun at View Skin Clinic, Seoul, viewskinclinic.com

Price
From about £2,500 to £5,500 for a full face and neck treatment

What Botulinum toxin (such as Botox or Xeomin), dermal filler and biostimulators are all used to sculpt, lift and plump, and can be combined in a “liquid facelift”. Biostimulators stimulate the skin’s collagen and elastin production, improving structure and firmness over time. Dermal filler, typically made from hyaluronic acid, restores volume. Botulinum toxin temporarily relaxes targeted muscles and can be deployed to lift the brows, slim the jawline and create a smoother appearance.

Who Biostimulators are a good entry point for those noticing the initial effects of ageing but don’t want intensive work. For hollowing under the eyes, cheeks and temples, or a loss of definition, dermal filler is ideal. Botulinum toxin is best for dynamic wrinkles – caused by repeated muscle movement – and can also lift brows that have begun to drop.

What to expect Most appointments take less than 30 minutes and downtime is minimal. But upkeep is required: botulinum toxin needs redoing every four months, dermal filler roughly every 18 months and biostimulators – which typically require three sessions about four weeks apart – every two years. Discomfort varies, but it isn’t much worse than having a quick injection. You may note some bruising or short-lived swelling.
Downsides Poor technique can result in an unnatural appearance, asymmetry or, in rare cases, vascular occlusion, leading to serious complications if not treated promptly.

Where
Dr Ashwin Soni at The Sonic Clinic, London, thesoniclinic.com
Dr Giulio Borbon at Studio Borbon, Milan, studioborbon.com
Dr Heyfa Ben Youssef, Paris, medecin-esthetiqueparis.com

Price
From about £300 up to £750

What A surgical procedure that involves removing or repositioning excess skin, fat or muscle on the upper or lower eyelids – or both – to create a refreshed eye area. It was the third most common cosmetic procedure in the UK in 2024 and its popularity continues to grow. It won’t alter the face’s contours dramatically, but it’s a fairly easy route to a more youthful appearance.

Who Anyone troubled by under-eye bags or hooded eyelids (where excess skin on the brow bone obscures the eyelid crease). It can also be suitable for anyone whose peripheral vision is affected by loose eyelid skin. Most practitioners recommend waiting until at least 40, when changes to the eye area start to become more noticeable.

What to expect A relatively low-pain procedure done under local anaesthetic. Exceptionally fine incisions are made along the eyelid’s natural crease and just below the lower lash line, meaning scarring is nearly imperceptible. Upper and lower lids can be treated in the same session. Each lid takes up to an hour, with some bruising, swelling, light sensitivity and numbness to be expected in the first weeks. Most patients see full results in around eight weeks. Improvements last until further skin sagging occurs due to ageing.

Downsides As with any surgery, there is a risk of bleeding and infection. Dry eyes, temporary numbness, double vision and difficulty closing the eyes can also occur. In some cases, changes in eyelid position or asymmetry may require revision surgery.

Where
Mr Naresh Joshi, London, cromwellhospital.com
Dr Mehryar Ray Taban, Beverly Hills, tabanmd.com
Dr Olivier Henry de Frahan, Paris, docteurolivierdefrahan.com

Price
From about £2,500 up to £8,000

What A single small incision made just above the ear or at the temples, discreetly placed within the hairline. From there, a suture (stitch) is anchored into the SMAS layer – the same connective tissue targeted by Ultherapy – to suspend and elevate the mid-face, lifting areas such as the cheekbones and jawline for a subtly contoured appearance.

Who Best approached as an early intervention, the one-stitch lift occupies a middle ground between injectables and major surgery – most suitable for under-50s beginning to notice gravity’s pull on the face (early jowls, a slackening jawline). Those with more extensive laxity may find its scope limited; the smaller incision can only address mild cases.

What to expect The procedure’s name is due to the fact it can be performed within 45 minutes. It is done under local anaesthetic, meaning same-day discharge is standard. Expect some bruising and swelling, which typically returns to normal within 10 days. Results last between three and five years.
Downsides Less common complications include skin puckering around the stitches, asymmetry, raised scarring and infection. In rare cases, facial nerve injury can cause temporary numbness or weakness.

Where
Dr Renato Calabria, Beverly Hills, Palm Springs and Milan, drcalabria.com
Mr Tunç Tiryaki, Istanbul and London, tunctiryaki.co.uk
Dr Ramtin Kassir, New York City and New Jersey, drkassir.com

Price
From about £3,500 up to £19,000

What The ponytail lift – also known as an endoscopic brow lift – takes its name from the snatched, eye-opening effect it can achieve. A surgeon uses a minuscule camera mounted on a thin tube to see and reposition the SMAS layer and deeper tissues without the need for large incisions.

Who Anyone whose eyebrows have descended, cheeks have fallen or who is experiencing a loss of youthful definition around the eyes or jaw. It suits those with robust, healthy skin – with good elasticity – who are in their late 30s to 50s and want to look younger without extensive surgery.

What to expect The endoscopic technique reduces visible scarring and the initial recovery period – which is often managed with prescription pain medication – lasts about one to two weeks. Performed under local or general anaesthetic as a day procedure, the surgery takes around 90 minutes, with stitches removed about a week later. Most patients see their final results within three to six months, lasting anywhere from five to 12 years.

Downsides Best suited to early signs of ageing; those with significant drooping, heavy jowling or excess neck skin are likely better served by a full facelift. Recovery typically involves bruising and swelling, while the risks of surgery include bleeding, infection, asymmetry and, in rare cases, temporary facial nerve weakness.

Where
Dr Chia Chi Kao, Santa Monica, kaoplasticsurgery.com
Dr Tim J Janssen at Waterhouse Janssen, London, waterhousejanssen.com
Dr Sam Rizk, New York City, drsamrizk.com

Price
From about £6,000 up to £190,000

What Unlike earlier methods that focused solely on tightening the skin, often creating results that looked overly stretched, the SMAS facelift focuses on treating the deeper structural layers of the face. It repositions the SMAS layer – made up of muscle, fat and connective tissue – before lifting the skin itself. It links the facial muscles responsible for expression to the skin above. By addressing this underlying structure, surgeons can create more defined contours while preserving natural movement.

Who Those with significant signs of ageing – pronounced jowls, a loose jawline, deep nasolabial folds or excess skin on the neck. The majority are in their 50s, 60s or beyond. Kris Jenner reportedly had one in 2025.

What to expect Incisions are made within the hairline and around the natural contours of the ear to keep scarring as imperceptible as possible. The procedure takes up to four hours and may require an overnight hospital stay. Recovery is gradual – swelling and bruising are to be expected in the first two weeks, and it can take three to six months for the tissue to settle into its new position. The results, however, are significant. Some claim to look a decade younger, with results lasting upwards of 10 years.

Downsides Beyond the expected downtime, there is a risk of delayed wound healing, bleeding, persistent swelling and changes to the skin’s contours. Rarer still, skin necrosis (the death of skin tissue), permanent numbness, facial nerve injury and complications related to anaesthesia are worth bearing in mind.

Where
Dr Steven Levine, New York City, stevenlevinemd.com
Dr Rajiv Grover, London, rajivgrover.co.uk
Dr Yannis Alexandrides at 111 Harley St, London, 111harleystreet.com

Price
From about £10,000 up to £190,000

What Widely considered to be the most advanced facial rejuvenation procedure available. Building on the principles of the SMAS facelift, this goes a step further by releasing the ligaments that anchor the facial tissues to the underlying bone. As these ligaments weaken over time, the cheeks, jawline and neck begin to descend. By carefully releasing and repositioning the deeper layers of tissue as a single unit – including the SMAS – the procedure targets the underlying causes of facial ageing rather than simply tightening the surface.
Who Most candidates are in their 50s, 60s or beyond; the SMAS and deep plane facelifts are generally presented as alternatives rather than complements.

What to expect The deep plane procedure takes up to four hours and incisions are made around the natural contours of the ears and within the hairline. Because the surgery works at such a deep level, fewer superficial nerve endings are disrupted, so patients are more likely to experience a feeling of tightness and pressure rather than significant pain. While early improvements are visible within weeks, many patients find the face continues to refine and heal for up to a year after surgery.

Downsides The surgery carries broadly the same risks as an SMAS procedure but, because it is more extensive and involves deeper tissue dissection, the potential for complications is slightly higher. But when performed by an experienced surgeon, it is considered a safe procedure with low complication rates.

Where
Mr Georgios Orfaniotis, London, orfaniotis.co.uk
Dr Min-Hee Ryu, Seoul and Beijing, psryuminhee.com
Dr Andrew Jacono at New York Center for Facial Plastic & Laser Surgery, newyorkfacialplasticsurgery.com

Price
From about £15,000 up to £190,000

title: The Gen Z-ers saving their parents’ fashion shops on TikTok
articleContent: It’s a sticky Tuesday evening in Shoreditch, east London, as shoppers squeeze past tightly packed shelves of leather bags and shoes at The Rich Collection Bella Italia. Someone exclaims “Y2K-esque like heck!” as women wearing vintage Gucci bags and denim miniskirts pick up rainbow kitten heels and their matching clutches, with their phones still in hand.

The footfall is impressive for a shop that was set to close at the end of summer. That is, until TikToker Caroline Rivier posted a video about The Rich Collection’s trove of “hidden treasure” shoes in late June, and caught the attention of the store owner’s daughter Zineb Lazraq. In the process, they unwittingly kicked off one of the most wholesome fashion trends of the season — the next generation posting their parents’ stores on social media to compel peers to show up and shop.

Lazraq (25), who previously had not spent much time in the store, was inspired to post her own “day-in-the-life” video of it in early July, which went viral. “It blew up overnight,” she says. “And then when the queue started forming, I thought, I need to be there to help my dad out.” With no retail experience, she was kept on her toes serving a two-hour-long queue.

Dad Rachid (59) has run The Rich Collection for three decades and seen the colourful row of leather stores on Hackney Road slowly become coffee roasters and craft breweries as the effects of Covid, rising rent and the cost-of-living crisis have taken their toll.

Thanks to a social media miracle, The Rich Collection is now serving thousands of new customers (many of whom also share their own shopping experience online) and the “Closing Down” sign was removed in mid-July — to cheers from those forming a queue. While there is now typically only a line on Saturdays, Lazraq and her sister Maryam (19) still help out in store, and they’ve hired a part-time shop assistant. Demand is still growing online, and Lazraq is working on a website and Vinted profile to reach shoppers worldwide.
Lazraq continues to post dispatches, often playing up the store’s “Y2K” aesthetic (a popular keyword and hashtag on TikTok), and her father also makes cameo appearances, talking through his smile.

For the first time in six years, The Rich Collection has introduced three new styles — heeled summer sandals — which it developed with its manufacturer in Naples, Italy. “When I see customers happy, it really makes me happy, and that motivates me,” says Rachid. “I think in the future, they’re going to see a lot more style, a lot more designs.”
A crowd of people gathers outside the Rich Collection shoe shop, with shoes displayed in the window

Inspired by The Rich Collection, comedian and actress Savannah Gracey changed up the usual sketches on her Instagram and TikTok for an earnest post about her mother Janet Dervan’s vintage store, The Arc, in mid-July. Gracey was moved to tears while showing her 243,000 followers (combined across Gracey’s social media platforms) the store in London’s Camden Market as it was preparing to close down.

“I wanted to help my mum out,” says Gracey (26), standing next to a row of silk and satin scarves still for sale on closing weekend. “She went to cry, and I was like, for goodness’ sake, get yourself together. And that’s what kicked it all off really,” adds Dervan (63). “And [since] then it’s been an absolutely joyous two weeks.”

During the interview, shoppers stop between the racks of Laura Ashley floral dresses to say hello to Gracey. Others subtly take photos of the 1960s tweed sets hanging up high. “Everyone is loving the story,” she says. “Everyone wants to be a part of it.”

Like Rachid Lazraq, Dervan also opened her first store three decades ago — in London’s Camden Market. She remembers working the till when Gracey was six weeks old, and selling clothes to Helena Bonham Carter, Debbie Harry and Boy George. She relocated The Arc a few times and opened her last shop in the Stables, 11 years ago. After experiencing low trade, high rent and additional service charges, Dervan decided not to renew her lease this year.

While the store did close in early August, Gracey’s videos have given her mum new hope. The Arc’s Vinted account has just over 2,000 followers and its new TikTok has 12,000 followers, to whom Dervan will post about future market appearances. “She’s set me up to be able to trade in the future,” says Dervan. “I didn’t realise how transferable her skills are, that she can just come in and just save the company.”

While they are two different stories, the success behind these viral video campaigns shows not only the social media engagement skills of Gen Z but also how emotional shopping can be. “What makes it a unique selling point is when there’s a very, very human angle behind it,” says Erifili Gounari (26), the founder and chief executive of Gen Z-led marketing agency The Z Link, over a video call. “It hits our empathetic nerves, and then we feel a lot more inclined to go and support.”
The Arc Textile & Clothing Company owner's daughter shares a guide on how friends, neighbours and the wider internet can support their shop during its closure

In a similar vein, Chaewon Kim (31), who goes by Chaey, is helping her mother, Mijeong Jung (59), with her Kool Kitten label — earnestly sharing social media videos about helping her mother reach a new audience online, while building a community around its concept store in New York.

Jung has worked in the fashion industry for more than 30 years; she founded her newest fashion label in South Korea in 2023. With girlish styles, it’s an ode to her two daughters, who lived out her dream by attending Parsons School of Design in New York. The Kool Kitten store in SoHo stocks 20 different labels, including Kim’s own Popsiz, and has already met its initial revenue goals.

“I started helping my mom because I could see how much the industry had changed,” says Kim, typing on her laptop in Seoul where she is preparing next season’s collection. “I wanted to help preserve what she’s spent her whole life building while bringing it into a new generation.”

It’s the younger generation’s belief in their parents that will see this through. “There’s something about the way that they see their parents that makes them able to communicate that same view of them to us, and that tends to feel a lot more precious,” says marketing expert Gounari.
“It’s not something I feel obligated to do,” adds Kim. “It’s something I genuinely feel lucky to do.”

Back at The Rich Collection, Zineb is musing on the success of her videos for her now family-run business. “If I could start any trend, then [this] sounds like a great one to start,” she says. “It’s actually having a real-world impact.”

title: Does your home need mothering? Call the house doula
articleContent: Artist Ashley Longshore has a hectic schedule. She juggles time painting in her studio with trips between her farm in Louisiana and her New York apartment, as well as visits with collectors around the country. It’s unpredictable day to day and, to help her, Longshore has plenty of staff on her roster — a housekeeper and an executive assistant, for example. But 64-year-old Manon Chevallerau fills a different niche, one that’s both nurturing and efficient. “Manon repots my orchids, organises my bras by colour and restocks my favourite lip balm. She also looks out for me — she nurtures me in a way,” Longshore explains. She calls Chevallerau by turns “a fairy godmother” and “a house doula”.

Dutch-born and NYC-based, Chevallerau started her doula career working with expectant mothers; she has repurposed those skills into an entirely different kind of at-home care. “I create a calm environment so that a person can be relaxed and start the day with everything in order,” she says. It’s what falls through the cracks between personal assistant, cleaner and house manager — a kind of mum-on-demand. “I need to be mothered,” says Longshore, matter-of-factly.

For the past 18 months, Chevallerau has come to Longshore’s apartment twice weekly for a few hours to handle whatever’s needed — organising closets, packing and unpacking suitcases, ferrying items to the dry cleaner. “I nurture the house and the person who’s in it, emotionally and practically,” she explains of the remit. “Support is what a doula does with a person, but now I do it with a home with the person in it.”

In London, Simmi Sangha fulfils a similar role. She’s the house doula for 50 or so clients of Eccord, the property management company; Sangha has wrangled the wrinkles of their private lives for the past five years. Demand has grown, so she now has a colleague working alongside her. Sangha’s background is as an estate agent but most of Eccord’s clients already have a housekeeper; the support they need is subtly different. She likens a house doula to a lifestyle manager for wealthy, time-poor types. “It’s someone to alleviate the stress of the little details,” Sangha explains.

Sangha has hunted for the lost engagement ring of a client who messaged from a taxiing plane; she walked round to her house and reassured her she’d left it on the bedside table. “My clients can ring me at any point of the day,” she says. Another called recently when her son clambered out of a swimming pool with bloodshot eyes. “I said, ‘Let’s not worry about the pH levels in the pool — has he put sun cream on today? That’s the problem,” Sangha continues. “We’re like human Google.”

That is the best description of the house doula-like role that a self-described high-profile “art world family” needed to fill three years ago; its 800-word “help wanted” ad quickly went viral. For the position, with an annual salary starting at $65,000, “the ideal candidate must be dedicated to a simple goal: make life easier for the couple in every way possible” and must have the ability to “seamlessly juggle multiple priorities in a dynamic, unstructured environment”.

The ad was quickly pulled from circulation following the backlash, but not before it caught Roshan Sethi’s eye. The doctor-turned-director, who co-created the hit TV series The Resident, was intrigued. He took it as inspiration for his just-released first novel The Simp. The darkly comic romp focuses on anti-hero Raj, a jobbing actor keen to use his new position as all-round household helpmeet with a Hollywood power couple to secure his on-screen stardom. But his Machiavellian efforts backfire for everyone.

“House doula is such a great phrase for what he’s doing,” says Sethi. “For many assistants, the description is just as nebulous, far-ranging and intersects with so many aspects of [their employer’s] lives.” The Canadian of Indian descent notes that the rise of such catchall roles is a model on which many Indian households have long relied. “It’s common there to have a servant who does all-encompassing jobs.” He adds that such a role was traditionally “way beyond what you could ask any American to do”. But that’s changing in the US. “As the rich get richer, people are on a train that cannot be stopped,” when it comes to how much help they expect and demand.
Recommended

Sethi’s novel spotlights this new role as a springboard for a nightmarish farce, but Longshore paints Chevallerau’s role as utterly indispensable: “She’s been working for 27 years to prepare herself for her one and only woman-child. I didn’t realise how much I needed her in my life, but she’s one of the greatest things I’ve ever allowed myself.”

The old asbestos town at the heart of the rare earths race
articleContent: For decades the remote town of Minaçu thrived off its asbestos mine, the last in the Americas, before the one-time miracle material’s links to deadly diseases led to bans and an industry decline.

Today, the municipality deep in Brazil’s interior is at the centre of a global race for the rare earth minerals essential to electronics, clean energy and defence tech, which have become a flashpoint in the US-China trade war.

In a wilderness of green peaks and valleys, a mining group claims to have the only site outside Asia digging up some of the scarcest types of these metals at scale, with financial backing from Washington.

Residents believe it can revive the fortunes of this community of 27,000 in the tropical savannah state of Goiás. Since commercial rare earths production in the South American country began here a couple of years ago, newcomers are arriving again, said Minaçu’s mayor Carlos Alberto Leréia.
“It’s a tremendous gain. The place was on its way to becoming a ghost town,” he added. “It’s as if you’re drowning and then a rope appears – you have to grab hold of it.”

The sentiment echoes wider optimism about Brazil’s potential to be a major player in a strategically important sector. Though its output remains modest for now, the country possesses the second-largest rare earth reserves after China, according to the US Geological Survey.
A group of 17 metallic elements required in small quantities for many high-tech applications, rare earths are relatively abundant in the planet’s crust but difficult to extract and separate.

With control over much of the world’s rare earth mining and a virtual monopoly on their processing, Beijing restricted exports last year in retaliation against President Donald Trump’s tariffs, intensifying a hunt for new sources.

That search has brought the Americans to Minaçu, where the mine’s owner Serra Verde is scaling up. “The objective is to be an alternative in the West for the production of rare earths,” said sustainability director Pedro Burnier at the company’s complex, which has received more than a billion dollars in investment.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.
USA Rare Earth, in which Washington owns a minority stake, announced a $2.8bn takeover of Switzerland-based Serra Verde in April.

“The rest of the world will [now] have access to the heavy rare earths that, quite frankly, we are all too dependent on China for today,” USA Rare Earth’s outgoing chief executive, Barbara Humpton, told the FT.
The project has also secured more than $500mn in loans from the US International Development Finance Corporation, a public lender.

The mine has become a linchpin of US efforts to break free of Chinese dominance over the minerals, thanks to the presence of two of the most critical heavy rare earths, so-called because of their higher atomic weight. Dysprosium and terbium are found in powerful magnets for guided missiles, electric vehicle motors and wind turbines, helping maintain magnetic strength at high temperatures.
“They are today the most highly valued,” said Burnier.

By next year, Serra Verde aims to account for more than half the heavy rare earth elements supply outside China. Yet its production target of 6,400 tonnes of total rare earth oxides still represents just a fraction of the overall 390,000 tonnes mined globally in 2025, according to USGS figures.

During construction, the company signed long-term supply deals with buyers in China, reflecting the lack of rare earth processing elsewhere, but later slashed their contract periods. Instead, Serra Verde now has a 15-year agreement to sell its output to an entity backed by the US government and private capital. This will then allocate stocks to processors, with guaranteed minimum prices in case China floods the market.
“Costs here are higher than in China, possibly due to our greater focus on environmental concerns,” said Fernando Landgraf, professor of metallurgical engineering at the University of São Paulo.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

American officials have long eyed Brazil’s critical minerals. However, as US-Brazil diplomatic relations have plunged over trade and political disputes, the Serra Verde offtake arrangement weakens Brasília’s negotiating power with Washington, according to Rob Muggah, co-founder of think-tank Igarapé Institute in Rio de Janeiro.
“The most serious concern is that the agreement could deprive Brazil of the feedstock needed to build its own rare earth industry,” added Muggah.

Ahead of a re-election bid in October, leftwing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has framed the resources as a matter of national sovereignty and wants his country to develop value-added manufacturing around the minerals, rather than just export raw materials. His main opponent, rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, has pledged closer co-operation with the US on the metals.
Serra Verde said it already undertakes significant processing in Minaçu, turning the clays into an intermediate substance containing light and heavy rare earths.
However, the next industrial step — separating the elements into high-purity individual oxides — is more difficult. New refineries are planned by companies in Europe, North America and Australia.

With scant arable land and limited industry around Minaçu, locals hope rare earths will help the area move on. The legacy of asbestos is visible from artificial terraced hills of mining waste that loom over the town’s streets.
Founded in the 1960s, the mine has stopped and restarted since Brazil’s Supreme Court banned asbestos use in 2017, but its closure is widely considered inevitable.

Thais Oliveira, an ice cream parlour owner, remembers hearing dynamite blasts and her mother’s stories of cleaning the dust that snowed down. Her sales are up about a quarter since Serra Verde started operations.

“The town was dead and there was nobody on the streets. Now it’s going back to what it was before,” said the 33-year-old mother.
However, not everyone is happy. Several residents said streams near Serra Verde had on occasion become discoloured with an oily residue after heavy downpours since the mine opened.
Smallholder Aníbal de Oliveira, 77, said: “The run-off is dirty. The water turns reddish because the soil is red up there.”

Serra Verde said it took “seriously any potential environmental impacts” and worked closely with regulators to identify and mitigate issues. It received a fine after self-reporting unlicensed deforestation in 2023.

The miner has 600 direct employees and hundreds of contractors, but some inhabitants wonder how far the benefits will spread. Hotel receptionist Nathanael Pereira Rodrigues took a course to train as a truck driver in anticipation of a vacancy, but is yet to be called.
“They only want skilled labour, with two or three years of experience,” said the 23-year-old soon-to-be father. “It’s frustrating, but I’m not going to give up.”

For all the hype around Brazil’s rare earths, Serra Verde’s long journey — roughly 15 years from first survey to shipment — shows the bureaucratic and financial hurdles that face such projects. Others are under development, though entrepreneurs often lament scarce funding and environmental permitting times.

Even so, mayor Leréia remains bullish: “Brazil is going to become a top player in rare earths.”

Additional reporting by Camilla Hodgson and Beatriz Langella. Data visualisation by Andrew Francisco and cartography by Chira Fae Llarena

title: Iranians queue for petrol as US blockade bites
articleContent: Long queues have formed at petrol stations around Tehran as the US blockade triggers fuel shortages and spreads alarm among motorists in a sign of the war’s growing strain on the Iranian economy.

The rush comes as Donald Trump’s administration outlined a new campaign of what it called “economic warfare” against Tehran, which the Energy Optimisation Organisation — an Iranian state body tasked with managing fuel resources — warned was facing a “critical” shortfall of petrol.

One petrol station attendant in the capital reported that people were rushing to fill up “even before their tanks are empty because they worry that the war might start over again or that prices will rise”. A limit of 20 litres per car meant that motorists had to keep returning, said the attendant, who did not want to be named.

The country, a major crude exporter, has long relied on petrol imports to make up the shortfall in its supplies. But the US naval blockade — in place since July 14 — has severely curtailed Iran’s ability to secure fuel, while the US and Israeli bombing campaign destroyed some of its refining capacity in the early weeks of the war, which began in February.
The EOO said Iran was currently 15mn litres short of its total daily petrol demand of 135mn.

US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that Washington was expanding the scope of secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners as it sought to tighten the economic and financial noose on Tehran.
The regime insists that Iran is able to resist US pressure and has refused to agree to Trump’s demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Both sides accuse each other of violating a June deal designed to gradually reopen the critical waterway and lay the foundation for talks over a final settlement, and Iran’s leaders argue that Tehran must inflict a greater cost on Washington before agreeing to end the war.
Imports from northern routes have also become severely constrained due to the effects of the Ukraine war and Russian losses of a significant portion of its refining capacity.

Iranian officials say the fuel shortage has been exacerbated by a subsidy system that provides the country’s 90mn population with some of the world’s cheapest petrol, with motorists charged between IR15,000 ($0.0075) and IR50,000 per litre.

The government, which has spent months tapping into Iran’s strategic reserves, says the current pricing and quota mechanism is no longer sustainable due to soaring inflation and the supply disruptions caused by the war.

President Masoud Pezeshkian said this month that selling petrol at below-market prices placed immense pressure on government resources required for food subsidies and support for workers. “Who said the government should buy petrol at 1.3mn rials per litre and then sell it for 15,000 rials?” he said.
And Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei, the head of Pezeshkian’s office, said Monday that the government intended to reduce quotas but that a final decision on pricing had not been made.

“There are uncertainties regarding the social, economic and security implications of any pricing policy,” he said, adding that while the government would definitely reduce quotas, “people may have to pay higher prices for consumption beyond their allocated quotas”.
But the prospect of raising fuel prices for a population whose purchasing power is weaker than ever is deeply sensitive.
Iran’s national currency has plunged to a new low of IR2mn to the dollar in recent days, with year-on-year inflation at nearly 90 per cent and food inflation at about 130 per cent.

A pilot project to increase petrol prices in Kerman province this month was halted just a few hours after its implementation. Suggestions of price rises recall memories of 2019, when an overnight increase triggered deadly protests across Iranian cities.
Petrol prices were a kind of “barometer of inflation” and liable to cause a very severe shock to the economy, said Morteza Behrouzifar, an energy analyst based in Tehran.
Behrouzifar suggested that the government continued short-term supply measures while trying to improve public transport, the domestic automotive industry and the refining industry.

“People are already under tremendous pressure,” he said. “If the government now wants to address this issue through an increase in petrol prices, it could have undesirable social and economic consequences.”

title: Bessent takes on bond vigilantes in $32tn Treasury market
articleContent: Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s bid to prop up the US bond market has been dismissed by investors as a “band-aid on a bullet hole”, as concerns mount over Washington’s $40tn debt burden and smouldering inflation.
The US Treasury department on Wednesday stunned Wall Street by revealing plans to “at least double” its purchases of long-term government bonds beginning next month.
Long-dated Treasuries soared after the announcement, pulling 30-year borrowing costs away from the 19-year high they reached days earlier.

But the rally quickly fizzled, with yields once again rising higher even after Bessent on Thursday took to CNBC television to tout the “big toolkit” at his disposal to tame the world’s most important market.

“[Bessent] understands the problem. But understanding the problem and being able to do something material about it are two different things,” said Jim Caron, chief investment officer at Morgan Stanley Investment Management. “The Treasury simply can’t control long-term yields.”

Bessent’s buyback strategy is the latest example of how the former hedge fund manager has taken a far more unconventional approach than many previous Treasury bosses. He has, in recent weeks, launched a rare move to boost the Japanese yen by selling euros and has repeatedly moved oil prices by signalling imminent progress in negotiations with Iran.

His attempt to cast himself as America’s “top bond salesman” has pitted him against bond vigilantes in the $32tn market — investors who have taken fright at America’s deteriorating public finances, persistently high inflation and the borrowing binge by Big Tech to finance the AI boom.
Charlie McElligott at Nomura said Bessent’s Treasury buyback plan “by itself” amounted to a “band-aid on a bullet hole” and would “not be enough to placate market forces”.

The Treasury said on Wednesday that beginning on September 9 it would increase its regular purchases of Treasuries maturing between 10 and 30 years from $2bn to $4bn or more. It marked a big expansion of a scheme that was initially designed to help facilitate trading in older Treasuries.

Some analysts said the abrupt nature of the move, which came two weeks after the quarterly refunding announcement when the Treasury normally unveils its borrowing strategy, had dented the agency’s credibility.
“We do not think it is hyperbole to say that this break in communication strategy reduces the overall credibility of their guidance,” said Thomas Simons, chief US economist at Jefferies.

Although Bessent did not spell it out, most investors expect the Treasury to balance higher buybacks of long-term securities by issuing more short-term debt — a move that leaves the department exposed to fluctuations in interest rates. It has not gone unnoticed that Bessent in 2024 criticised then Treasury secretary Janet Yellen for pursuing a similar policy.

“The question is will Bessent continue to go down the path he criticised,” said Mike O’Rourke at Jones Trading, who expects that the Treasury secretary will be forced to be “bigger and more aggressive” if he plans to continue “papering over the problems”.

Bessent argued on Thursday that “yields don’t reflect the underlying fundamentals”, citing the effects of the Iran war and “very poor” liquidity in the 30-year Treasury market. He said Washington would announce at the end of this week or early next week “an increased focus on fiscal consolidation”, while adding that there is a “very good chance” the US has reached the peak of its government deficits.

The non-partisan Congressional Budget Office projects the US budget deficit will register 5.8 per cent this year — steady compared with 2025 and well above Bessent’s long-stated goal of reaching 3 per cent by 2028.

Sarah Bianchi at Evercore said that “while Bessent’s comments signal a focus on fundamental drivers of high borrowing costs, we are sceptical the administration can realistically do anything at this point on the deficit that would be material”.
“The surprise buybacks announcement this week has had only a fleeting effect, and we think any deficit-related announcement would be at least as limited,” she said.

Scott DiMaggio, head of fixed income at AllianceBernstein, said that for the buyback to have a more lasting effect, “you need the [Federal Reserve] to do something. And then you have to do something on the deficit side and the debt management side too.”
Others stressed that Bessent’s higher buyback plan was designed to demonstrate the Treasury’s concern and slow the rise in bond yields rather than reverse the move higher altogether.
Robert Tipp, head of global bonds at PGIM, argued the US bond market sell-off would have been more pronounced without Bessent’s intervention.

“It’s a finger in the dike, but you’re in a world of rising interest rates, fiscal profligacy and above-target inflation, and frankly the US has been an outperformer” compared with other countries’ bond markets, Tipp said.

title: Nvidia employee charged with smuggling advanced chips into China
articleContent: An Nvidia employee has been charged in Taiwan with smuggling advanced AI chips into China in the first known indictment of a worker at the US chipmaker over alleged illegal exports.
Taiwan’s Keelung District Prosecutors’ Office charged nine people, including employees of server maker Super Micro Computer, on Monday with illegally selling high-end AI servers to Chinese customers.
Prosecutors accused the defendants of colluding in pursuit of huge profits and “seriously damaging Taiwan’s international image”. Many of Nvidia’s chips and servers are made in Taiwan.
They described a Taiwan-based senior manager at Nvidia surnamed Zhang as the “central figure” in a scheme involving 130 of the chipmaker’s flagship B300 servers.

The B300 is a popular server for training AI models and contains Nvidia’s advanced chips. The servers are subject to US export controls as Washington tries to constrain China’s ability to develop cutting-edge AI.
Washington’s restrictions have created a lucrative black market under which prices can double or triple.

Prosecutors said Zhang, two senior Super Micro salespeople, a Taiwanese distributor and other intermediaries colluded to circumvent customer checks by both Nvidia and Super Micro, which is one of several companies that package Nvidia’s AI chips into servers.
They alleged that defendants falsely claimed the servers would be used in a data centre in Taiwan, even though its electricity supply and network bandwidth were insufficient to operate them.

Of the 130 servers, 74 were ultimately shipped to Chinese customers, according to prosecutors, either directly from Taiwan or routed through Indonesia or Japan. The remaining 56 were stopped by Taiwan customs officials.

Zhang allegedly helped secure an allocation of servers and participated in an inspection of the data centre where they would purportedly be used.
Prosecutors said he deliberately concealed that the data-centre buyer lacked sufficient financial resources and that the funds used to purchase the servers actually came from a Chinese company.
They have requested the statutory maximum sentence of five years in prison for Zhang and three other defendants, while the other five were recommended for shorter terms.

An Nvidia spokesperson said: “Our employees have every incentive to work diligently with customers to ensure compliance with all applicable laws. We will work with the Taiwan authorities to help them resolve the allegations as quickly as possible.”

Super Micro said its “co-operation with Taiwanese authorities led to the arrests of the indicted individuals” and that it was “not a target of their investigation and has not been accused of any wrongdoing”.
Additional reporting by Michael Acton in San Francisco

title: SEC subpoenas Wall Street banks over Situational Awareness
articleContent: The Securities and Exchange Commission has subpoenaed some of the largest Wall Street banks that helped fund trading bets at Situational Awareness before the hedge fund was nearly toppled in the recent tech sell-off.

The US financial markets regulator requested detailed information about Situational Awareness’s trades and its communication with the lenders that provided it with leverage, according to two people familiar with the probe.

The hedge fund was a client of Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Citigroup and Bank of America, according to regulatory filings. Lending to hedge funds has become an increasingly important and lucrative business line for Wall Street banks in recent years.

The AI-focused hedge fund run by 24-year-old OpenAI alumnus Leopold Aschenbrenner amassed more than $20bn in assets in less than two years and racked up astronomical gains, using borrowed money to amplify its concentrated bets on AI-linked stocks.

Situational Awareness ran into difficulty during the intense tech sell-off in July, becoming the biggest casualty of the market downswing. After facing steep losses, the San Francisco-based firm was forced to sell the majority of its stock holdings to Citadel in an emergency transaction pulled together in just 24 hours.

“It is to be expected that regulators would closely examine any funds that are high-profile, produce significant returns, or have particularly dramatic drawdowns,” Situational Awareness said in a statement. “We are a highly regulated business and will co-operate to the fullest extent with any regulatory request.”
Recommended
The fund has not been accused of wrongdoing. One person cautioned that the SEC probe was simply in the “information-gathering” stage.
Citigroup, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan declined to comment. The SEC also declined to comment.

In the aftermath of the deal with Citadel, Aschenbrenner has said he took “full responsibility” for the events that led to the rapid losses. He said the fund would continue to operate and trade public equities but would no longer borrow from banks to fund his bets.

Citadel purchased the positions at a roughly 10 per cent discount, the FT has previously reported. Earlier this month, Ken Griffin’s hedge fund told investors the firm had sold more than 80 per cent of the portfolio via almost 100 block trades worth more than $4bn.
The New York Times first reported the subpoenas.
Additional reporting by Kaye Wiggins

title: Anthropic’s best AI model struggles to attract users as cheaper tools thrive
articleContent: Anthropic’s US customers are using cheaper alternatives to its most powerful AI tool, raising questions about the group’s high-spending business model ahead of what is expected to be the biggest initial public offering of all time.

Spending on Fable 5, Anthropic’s largest and priciest model, has plateaued at only about 11 per cent of overall outlay on the company’s tools, more than two months after its release, according to spending data from 70,000 companies collected by payments group Ramp.

This breaks a pattern of corporate users defaulting to the most powerful models. Analysts and investors in Anthropic said the change was primarily driven by Fable’s high price and the fact that older models are capable of handling the bulk of business demands.

If sustained, the shift could radically alter the business model of frontier labs, which have until now funnelled the bulk of their multibillion-dollar development spending towards training larger, more sophisticated models.

“Most people don’t need to operate at the frontier,” said Miles Clements, a partner at Accel, which has invested close to $1bn in Anthropic. The period in which customers tended to choose only the frontier models “was not a durable era”, he added.

Breakthroughs in intelligence remain essential to fulfil the companies’ loftiest promises, such as curing disease, and to attract the best researchers. But they will increasingly be showcases, said Clements.
Fable 5’s launch in early June was disrupted by Donald Trump’s administration, which forced Anthropic to withdraw the model, citing national security concerns.

Concerns about further limits on access to Fable have receded since the White House greenlit its relaunch on July 1. Political uncertainty has become a secondary factor, compared with price and performance, in driving clients’ model choice, according to analysts and investors.

The lower demand for Fable, which has had a slower rate of take-up than previous cutting-edge releases, adds to the uncertainty for Anthropic ahead of its IPO, which investors anticipate will value the group at $2tn or more and could come as soon as next month.

Anthropic’s revenue in July undershot the most bullish expectations from investors, who projected annualised sales would cross $80bn. Anthropic told shareholders last week that its revenue last month hit $65bn on an annualised basis, up from $47bn in May.
Still, the start-up led by chief executive Dario Amodei continues to grow at a blistering pace, with revenue increasing nearly sevenfold since the start of the year.

Anthropic recorded its first adjusted operating profit in the second quarter of the year and has guided investors that it is likely to be profitable again in the third quarter, according to people with knowledge of the matter. It also told investors that it had 6,000 customers that spend $100,000 annually or more.
The company declined to comment.
Businesses are trying to contain spending on AI by using models more efficiently rather than always going with the most sophisticated option.

The availability of cheap, open-weight models from China and elsewhere has provided customers with more alternatives to the leading US labs, while there are also signs that Sam Altman’s OpenAI is gaining ground after slipping back for much of 2026.

The ChatGPT maker’s annualised revenue has jumped 35 per cent in the quarter to date and is now more than $40bn, with the launch of GPT 5.6 in July jolting the company’s performance after a sluggish start to the year, said people with knowledge of the matter.
Recommended

GPT 5.6 is priced significantly lower than Fable 5. Anthropic’s Opus 5, a smaller but nevertheless potent model that comes at a lower price, has surpassed Fable in terms of business spending since its launch in late July, according to Ramp.
Anthropic’s revenue growth took a hit in June, largely because of the US government’s decision to limit the rollout of Fable, but has since rebounded.
Data retention rules imposed by the Trump administration have also hampered Fable’s adoption, according to Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp.

Kharazian said predicting the company’s trajectory even months ahead is a virtually impossible task. “If you impute previous trends you expect Anthropic to own the market. But because [OpenAI’s newest model] was so good and Fable underperformed, it’s been the reverse,” he added.

title: US widens AI-driven investment gap with Europe
Waymo doubles spending on lobbying in robotaxi battle with Uber
articleContent: Waymo has sharply increased its lobbying spending as it seeks to persuade US regulators to clear a path for fully autonomous taxi services, intensifying its battle with rival Uber over the future of robotaxis.

The Alphabet-owned company spent more than $1mn between April and June on lobbying the federal government, more than double its outlay a year earlier, according to filings. That put Waymo’s spending close to Uber’s and well ahead of rivals including Amazon’s Zoox and Tesla.

The rise in lobbying comes as Waymo and Uber push competing visions for the future of ride-hailing. Waymo wants a faster route to fully driverless commercial services, while Uber is advocating a staggered rollout in which robotaxis operate alongside human drivers.

Their diverging legislative strategies have contributed to their relationship souring. The FT reported last month that Waymo was exploring options to exit its Uber partnership in Austin and Atlanta, where the ride-hailing group operates its services.
“They’ve both stepped up lobbying and are pushing up against each other, which now appears to be hastening their divorce,” said Walter Piecyk, an analyst at LightShed Partners.

Both companies are lobbying aggressively in several US states and Washington DC after pushback stalled their expansion to markets including New York and Chicago, as politicians and labour groups warn the technology could displace drivers and undercut existing services.

In the first six months of 2026, Waymo increased its spending by 93 per cent from the year before to slightly more than $2mn. It has called for a federal framework to ease the rollout of robotaxis. In May, it hired law firm Greenberg Traurig to lobby on its behalf, adding to a roster of several other Washington firms.

At the local level, the robotaxi operator has outspent both Uber and Zoox in lobbying legislators in the District of Columbia. It has pressed local regulators to allow robotaxi services in the nation’s capital, including by inviting residents earlier this year to write in support of its rollout.
In New York state, Waymo has spent more than half a million dollars so far this year — more than double Uber’s lobbying spend — as it seeks a foothold in one of the largest taxi markets.

Its lobbying in the state intensified after Governor Kathy Hochul earlier this year walked back proposals that would have allowed autonomous vehicle companies to run services across most of the state.
Waymo offered to set up a $20mn fund to support drivers affected by the technology’s deployment, according to people familiar with the matter.
In New Jersey, it has engaged lawmakers who are exploring a three-year pilot programme to test deployments.
Waymo said in a statement that it was advocating for the rollout of autonomous vehicles and was not pursuing measures that would limit competitors or “prescribe” how the technology was deployed.

Uber, meanwhile, has been racing to make up lost ground in AVs after abandoning its in-house self-driving effort in 2020, committing more than $10bn over the past year through equity stakes and robotaxi fleet agreements.

The ride-hailing group has warned several Democratic-led states against a carte blanche rollout and has instead lobbied for so-called hybrid networks that route rides to both human drivers and autonomous vehicles.

In New Jersey, Uber lobbyists have proposed that any platform offering robotaxi services also use human drivers for at least 85 per cent of all rides during a three-year pilot programme.

Critics have accused Uber of seeking regulatory capture by attempting to keep rides flowing through its platform as it grapples with rising competition.

Uber has said it is false that they were “anti-AV or seeking to slow AV deployment”. It said hybrid networks “get the technology to consumers sooner while giving policymakers a practical framework to manage the transition”.

title: Apple paid $17bn in taxes to Ireland after court ruling on back levies
articleContent: Apple paid Ireland $17bn in taxes last year, representing 40 per cent of its worldwide total, according to filings that offer new insight into the iPhone maker’s global tax liabilities.

The $17bn payment was significantly boosted after the EU’s top court in 2024 ordered Apple to pay €13bn in back taxes. The court ruled that Ireland had granted the tech giant “unlawful aid”, resulting in a tax rate of less than 1 per cent. Apple paid $43bn in corporate income taxes worldwide last year.

Ireland has reaped big windfalls due to its low corporate tax rate, which is 12.5 per cent at present. In 2024, just three companies — widely believed to be Eli Lilly, Apple and Microsoft — paid almost half of all corporation tax collected in the country.

Companies were lured to Ireland by a tax system that allowed them to route profits to tax havens through a structure known as the “double Irish”. The loophole was abolished in 2015 but the country retained many large US companies that had set up significant operations there.
A quarter of Apple’s global pre-tax profits in the year to September 2025 were booked through its Ireland entities, where it employs about 3 per cent of its workforce, according to the filings.

The latest figures were published under new EU rules that require large companies to break down revenues, profits and corporate income taxes for every jurisdiction in the bloc as well as designated tax havens.

Apple booked pre-tax profits of $6mn per employee in Ireland, compared with just $51,000 per employee in Germany, where it paid $153mn in cash taxes, or 0.3 per cent of its total. Apple employs 5,575 people in Ireland, which is home to its European headquarters, and 4,089 in Germany.
New tax disclosure measures are providing campaigners with fresh ammunition to push big businesses to boost their contributions to public finances.
Companies, however, have complained that the latest rules paint an incomplete and misleading picture of the contributions they make to individual countries.
Apple said it was “consistently one of the world’s largest taxpayers”.

It sought to draw a distinction between the corporate income taxes reported in the new filing, which it said are paid in jurisdictions where assets are held, and consumption taxes such as value-added taxes, which are paid where consumers are based.
Microsoft in June revealed that it had booked 38 per cent of its global pre-tax profit in Ireland last year, equivalent to more than $7mn per employee.

Procter & Gamble reported $115mn in profit and no tax in Luxembourg, where it had just one employee. The consumer goods group said it had ceased operations in the country and that it had paid no tax because it had offset profits last year with losses from previous years.

Beyond the EU, Australia is expected to release similar country-by-country breakdowns later this year, while new US accounting rules are forcing listed companies to specify in annual reports whether and how their overseas operations reduced their US tax bills.
In a sign of its concern, Microsoft accompanied its report with a blog post that acknowledged “strong views about whether companies are paying enough”.
It said a cash payment recorded from France’s tax authority “reflects a one-time refund of tax overpaid” and was “a good example of why a single line can look unusual without context”.
The National Foreign Trade Council, a Washington-based lobby group, cautioned that the EU rules could result in double counting of revenue when subsidiaries sell products to one another.
Additional reporting by Chris Cook

title: Samsung to return record $80bn to shareholders
articleContent: Samsung Electronics will return a record $80bn to shareholders through dividends and buybacks as the South Korean chipmaker faces pressure to distribute more of its bumper AI-driven profits.

The company said on Friday it would return Won90tn to Won110tn ($65bn to $80bn) to shareholders this year, depending on business performance, investment needs and cash flow. The programme, its largest ever, is about five times its 2020 payout, the previous record.
Samsung plans to buy back Won15tn of its shares from Monday until November 21 and pay about Won30tn in cash dividends in the third quarter.
It will decide on the remaining payouts for the fourth quarter next January, with options including cash dividends, further buybacks and share cancellations.

“This record-setting level of shareholder returns is intended to ensure that the benefits of the company’s growth are delivered to shareholders in a tangible way,” Samsung said, adding that it had balanced the payouts against its need to maintain growth.

Samsung’s move is part of a three-year commitment since 2024 to return half of its free cash flow to shareholders. It comes after its rival SK Hynix said this week it planned to repurchase Won40tn ($29bn) of shares and return more than half of its free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027 to shareholders.
Investors hope the distributions from the world’s two largest makers of memory chips will help calm concerns over the durability of AI spending.

Samsung and SK Hynix have enjoyed record profits from the build-out of AI data centres that use their semiconductors. Operating profit at Samsung jumped more than 12-fold year on year to more than $100bn in the first half, while that of SK Hynix rose fivefold to about $70bn. Analysts expect full-year combined operating profit to top $400bn.

But investors are beginning to question whether chip demand has reached a peak in a notoriously cyclical industry. Shares of Samsung and SK Hynix have fallen 22 per cent and 41 per cent respectively from their highs in June, though they are still up nearly fourfold and sevenfold in the past year.

Both companies have benefited from strong demand for high-bandwidth memory chips used in AI hardware. Their focus on the top-end products has contributed to shortages of more conventional semiconductors used in consumer electronics, pushing up chip prices across the board.
The bumper profits have intensified pressure on the chipmakers to share more of their windfall with investors.

Samsung chief financial officer Park Soon-cheol said during an earnings call last month that the company would seek to “find the optimal balance between maximising shareholder value and reinvestment for future growth”.
JPMorgan analysts expect SK Hynix to announce further shareholder returns of at least $130bn.

Analysts said the expanded distributions signalled that the companies were confident they had sufficient financial resources to shore up their share prices while increasing capital spending to meet AI-driven demand.
“The absolute amount looks big, but it is not such a sharp increase in proportion to the company’s strong earnings growth,” said Chaiwon Lee, chair of Seoul-based Life Asset Management.

“However, this shows the company has strong financial firepower to boost shareholder returns and help ease investor discontent,” he added. “The recent share price decline is not due to any change in fundamentals, but rather a pullback after a blistering rally earlier.”
